finding_title: Sec63 perturbation induces an ER-chaperone response distinct from selected secretory-pathway perturbations
main_reason: Confidence is moderate (3) based on well-established translocon biology involving SEC63 and the SEC61 channel in co-translational ER protein entry (Lang et al., 2012, PMID: 22375059; Lang et al., 2017, PMID: 29163222). Novelty is closely precedented (2) because ER translocation stress and unfolded protein response (UPR) activation via ATF4/CHOP/CHAC1 are known mechanisms. However, demonstrating a distinct chaperonin module (Hspa5, Canx, Hyou1, Chac1) in thalamic neurons that separates SEC63 loss from downstream secretory perturbations (Ssr4, Stt3b, Ergic1) is an important refinement. Support is plausible but incomplete (3) due to robust, statistically significant upregulation of the chaperone module (Hspa5 log2FC +0.924, FDR 6.31e-4; Chac1 log2FC +2.030, FDR 0.0179) in 151 TH neurons, though bounded by the lack of direct Sec63 self-transcript depletion and unmeasured translocon client protein accumulation. Priority is moderate (3) as it offers a clean translocon stress transcriptomic reporter, though broader impact depends on identifying specific neuronal client proteins.
excited_community:
Endoplasmic reticulum stress laboratories, translocon biophysics groups, unfolded protein response (UPR) researchers, and neurobiology laboratories studying secretory protein quality control.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. Richard Zimmermann (Saarland University) - SEC63/SEC61 translocon complex architecture, ER protein import kinetics, and chaperonin interactions.
b. Dr. Stefan Somlo (Yale University School of Medicine) - SEC63 molecular genetics, translocon function, and polycystic disease pathomechanisms.
c. Dr. David Ron (University of Cambridge) - UPR signaling cascades, PERK/ATF4 activation, and CHAC1 induction under ER stress.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform Western blotting and cycloheximide chase assays in primary thalamic neurons to quantify SEC63 protein depletion and client protein import kinetics into the ER lumen. Measure luminal versus cytosolic accumulation of specific secretome and transmembrane clients (e.g., chromogranins, neuropeptide Y, or ion channel subunits) using pulse-chase radiolabeling and subcellular fractionation. Evaluate UPR branch activation by measuring XBP1 mRNA splicing via RT-PCR and p-eIF2alpha / ATF4 protein levels via immunoblotting. Conduct live-cell fluorescence imaging with ER-targeted sensors (e.g., ER-GFP) and KDEL immunofluorescence to measure ER morphological expansion or fragmentation following Sec63 knockdown. Assess whether pharmacological UPR modulators (such as ISRIB or BiP inducers) rescue CHAC1-mediated pro-apoptotic signaling and neuronal cell death.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NIGMS/NINDS research project grants investigating translocon import stress, client protein specificity, and organellar UPR dynamics in neuronal homeostasis.

finding_title: NAA20 perturbation couples recurrent CYP46A1 repression to induction of sterol-synthesis transcripts
main_reason: Confidence is moderate (3) based on familiarity with co-translational N-terminal acetylation (NatB complex) and brain cholesterol elimination pathways via CYP46A1 (Petrov and Pikuleva, 2019, PMID: 31001737;  Deng et al., 2020, PMID: 32885784). Novelty is high (4) because while NAA20 loss is linked to human neurodevelopmental delay, connecting Naa20 perturbation to recurrent downregulation of the central neuronal cholesterol-eliminating enzyme Cyp46a1 across subcortical populations (151 TH, 155 MB, 191 MB) alongside compensatory sterol-synthesis induction (Fdft1, Cyp51) reveals an unexpected (unreported and non-obvious) metabolic axis. Support is plausible (3) due to consistent, highly significant Cyp46a1 downregulation (log2FC -0.39 to -1.04) paired with sterol gene elevation (Fdft1 log2FC +1.02, FDR 1.79e-5), though bounded (incomplete) by unmeasured N-terminal acetylation kinetics, CYP46A1 protein levels, or 24S-hydroxycholesterol flux. Priority is high (4) as it reframes NatB neurodevelopmental pathology around a novel NAA20-CYP46A1-sterol turnover axis, providing actionable metabolic and biomarker targets.
excited_community:
N-terminal acetyltransferase biochemists, brain lipid/cholesterol metabolism researchers, and neurodevelopmental disorder geneticists.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. Thomas Arnesen (University of Bergen) - NatB complex biochemistry, NAA20 catalytic activity, and human N-terminal acetyltransferase syndromes.
b. Dr. Ingemar Bjorkhem (Karolinska Institutet) - brain cholesterol turnover, CYP46A1 biochemistry, and 24S-hydroxycholesterol flux.
c. Dr. Nathalie Cartier (Inserm / CEA) - CYP46A1 gene therapy, neuronal cholesterol clearance, and neurodegenerative disease mechanisms.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform LC-MS/MS lipidomics in Naa20-depleted thalamic and midbrain neuronal cultures to directly measure intracellular cholesterol, lanosterol, and 24S-hydroxycholesterol levels. Execute N-terminal acetylomics (COFRADIC or SILAC-based acetyl-N-terminomics) to identify direct NatB substrates and test if unacetylated CYP46A1 undergoes accelerated proteasomal degradation. Measure CYP46A1 protein abundance and enzymatic activity using 24S-hydroxycholesterol generation assays. Conduct SREBP2 nuclear translocation assays via Western blot and immunofluorescence following Naa20 perturbation to confirm active transcription-factor-driven sterol pathway induction. Test whether exogenous 24S-hydroxycholesterol treatment or AAV-CYP46A1 rescue normalizes the sterol-synthesis gene induction (Fdft1, Cyp51) and preserves neuronal membrane integrity.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NINDS/NIGMS research initiatives on co-translational N-terminal acetylation (NatB), neuronal sterol flux, and CYP46A1 homeostasis in neurodevelopmental disorders".

finding_title: Elp1 perturbation activates an amino-acid starvation and integrated-stress-like program in thalamic glutamatergic neurons
main_reason: Confidence is high (4) based on knowledge of the Elongator complex (ELP1/IKBKAP) in tRNA wobble uridine modification (mcm5s2U) and familial dysautonomia genetics (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001, PMID: 11179008). Novelty is high (4) because ELP1 studies traditionally focus on peripheral sensory and autonomic neurodevelopment. Discovering that acute postmitotic Elp1 loss in central thalamic neurons triggers a massive amino acid starvation and Integrated Stress Response (ISR) program (Cars, Asns, Shmt2, Slc1a4, Ddit3) reveals an unexpected (unreported and non-obvious) subcortical vulnerability. Support is sound and well-grounded (4) with 570 changed genes in 151 TH neurons and outstanding statistical significance for aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and amino acid transporters (Cars log2FC +1.12, FDR 1.53e-28; Asns log2FC +1.46, FDR 1.50e-27; Slc1a4 log2FC +2.23, FDR 2.87e-21), though eIF2alpha phosphorylation and ATF4 protein levels were unmeasured. Priority is high (4) because it connects Elongator tRNA modification failure to codon-specific translation arrest and GCN2/ATF4 stress signaling in central subcortical circuits.
excited_community:
tRNA modification laboratories, translational control groups, familial dysautonomia researchers, and Integrated Stress Response (ISR) biophysicists.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. Susan Slaugenhaupt (Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard Medical School) - ELP1 genetics, RNA splicing, and familial dysautonomia pathomechanisms.
b. Dr. Francesc Posas (Institute for Research in Biomedicine - IRB Barcelona) - Elongator complex biochemistry, tRNA wobble modifications, and translational stress.
c. Dr. Sebastian Leidel (University of Bern) - tRNA modifications, ribosome translational speed, and Elongator-mediated stress signaling.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform LC-MS/MS on isolated tRNA from Elp1-perturbed thalamic neurons to quantify the loss of 5-carbamoylmethyluridine (ncm5U) and 5-methoxycarbonylmethyl-2-thiouridine (mcm5s2U) wobble modifications. Conduct ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) to identify codon-specific translational pausing at AAA, GAA, and CAA codons across the neuronal transcriptome. Perform Western blotting for phosphorylated eIF2alpha (p-eIF2alpha), ATF4, GCN2, and DDIT3/CHOP to confirm activation of the amino acid starvation branch of the Integrated Stress Response. Execute amino acid profiling via LC-MS to determine if intracellular free amino acid pools (e.g., asparagine, serine) are depleted following Elp1 loss. Test whether pharmacological ISR inhibitors (such as ISRIB) or AAV-mediated Elp1 cDNA rescue suppress ASNS/CARS induction and prevent thalamic neuronal death.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NINDS/NIGMS research project grants on elongator complex tRNA modification, ribosome stalling, and integrated stress response activation in central neuronal pathology.

finding_title: KMT2A perturbation reveals a mature thalamic Nr2f1-Pcdh7-Lhx9 maintenance state
main_reason: Confidence is moderate (4) based on knowledge of histone H3K4 methyltransferase genetics, Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome, and epigenetic regulation of neural plasticity (Jakovcevski et al., 2015, PMID: 25834037; Jones et al., 2012, PMID: 22795537). Novelty is modest (3) because KMT2A (MLL1) is well known for controlling embryonic HOX clusters, adult neural stem cell neurogenesis, and prefrontal synaptic plasticity. Demonstrating a postmitotic thalamic maintenance regulon (Nr2f1, Lhx9, Pcdh7) is an incremental functional extension of the known biology in a new context. Support is plausible (3) due to clear, directionally concordant transcript drops in 151 TH neurons (Nr2f1 log2FC -0.806, FDR 2.39e-10; Lhx9 log2FC -1.182; Pcdh7 log2FC -0.774), though limited to 24 FDR-passing genes in a single cell context without direct H3K4me3 CUT and RUN binding data or electrophysiological recordings. Priority is moderate (3) as it supplies a clean mature thalamic readout for testing epigenetic therapies in Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome models.
excited_community:
Chromatin epigenetics research groups, Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome geneticists, and neurobiology laboratories investigating histone methyltransferase activity in mature neuronal circuits.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. Schahram Akbarian (Friedman Brain Institute and Brudnick Neuropsychiatric Research Institute, University of Massachusetts Medical School) - KMT2A/MLL1 epigenetic regulation in postmitotic neuronal plasticity, histone H3K4 methylation, and cognition.
b. Dr. Hans Bjornsson (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and University of Iceland) - Wiedemann-Steiner syndrome genetics, Mendelian disorders of the epigenetic machinery, and chromatin remodeler therapies.
c. Dr. Daniel Lim (University of California, San Francisco) - KMT2A/MLL1 complexes in neural lineage specification and postnatal neurogenesis.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform CUT and RUN for KMT2A and H3K4me3 in purified postmitotic thalamic neurons to confirm direct chromatin occupancy at promoter and enhancer loci of Nr2f1, Lhx9, and Pcdh7. Conduct Western blotting and histone extraction assays to quantify global versus locus-specific H3K4me3 reduction following Kmt2a knockdown. Perform conditional postnatal Kmt2a deletion in thalamic glutamatergic neurons (using Otx2-CreERT2 or Syt6-Cre) followed by RNA-seq to confirm age-dependent maintenance requirements. Evaluate thalamocortical axon arborization and synaptic density in thalamic slices via immunofluorescence for Pcdh7 and VGLUT2. Test whether small-molecule histone demethylase inhibitors (e.g., KDM5 inhibitors) restore H3K4me3 levels and rescue Nr2f1/Pcdh7 expression in Kmt2a-deficient adult neurons.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NINDS/NIMH research grants on postmitotic chromatin maintenance and H3K4 methylation regulons in Mendelian disorders of the epigenetic machinery.

finding_title: MATR3 perturbation induces an RBP state that active FUS and TDP-43 perturbations do not reproduce
main_reason: Confidence is moderate (3) based on familiarity with nuclear RNA-binding proteins, alternative splicing networks, and MATR3 mutations in ALS and distal myopathy (Johnson et al., 2014, PMID: 24686783). Novelty is high (4) because while MATR3, FUS, and TDP-43 are all ALS-linked RBPs, discovering that acute Matr3 perturbation drives a highly recurrent, unique transcriptomic module (Atp9b, Ddhd1, E2f4 UP; Rsrp1 DOWN) across cortical, thalamic, and midbrain neurons that is not phenocopied by Fus or Tardbp knockdown proves that MATR3 depletion exposes a distinct RBP liability state rather than a generic ALS-RBP stress response. Support is sound and wel grounded (4) due to strong statistical significance across multiple independent cell classes (151 TH: Ddhd1 log2FC +1.77, FDR 2.64e-49; Rsrp1 log2FC -0.69, FDR 1.26e-29) with explicit negative control contrasts against Fus and Tardbp, though direct RNA-binding CLIP-seq and splicing isoform shifts remain to be mapped. Priority is high (4) as it establishes a distinct mechanistic and biomarker framework for MATR3-linked ALS and frontotemporal degeneration.
excited_community:
ALS and frontotemporal dementia research communities, RNA-binding protein biophysics laboratories, and neurodegenerative disease biomarker consortiums.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. J. Paul Taylor (St. Jude Children's Research Hospital) - MATR3 mutations, RBP dynamics, nucleocytoplasmic transport, and ALS pathomechanisms.
b. Dr. Bryan Traynor (National Institute on Aging, NIH) - MATR3 discovery in ALS/FTD genetics and human neurodegenerative genomics.
c. Dr. Sami Barmada (University of Michigan) - MATR3 RNA binding, nucleocytoplasmic transport, and neuronal toxicity models.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform enhanced cross-linking immunoprecipitation sequencing (eCLIP-seq) for MATR3, FUS, and TDP-43 in parallel from subcortical neurons to determine whether MATR3 directly binds 3-prime UTRs or introns of Atp9b, Ddhd1, and E2f4 pre-mRNAs. Conduct Nanopore long-read RNA sequencing to evaluate alternative splicing and intron retention events specific to MATR3 loss versus TDP-43/FUS loss. Perform Western blotting and immunofluorescence to measure protein abundance and subnuclear localization of E2F4 and RSRP1 following Matr3 knockdown. Conduct patch-clamp electrophysiology to evaluate M-currents driven by Kcnq2 upregulation in Matr3-deficient cortical and thalamic neurons. Test whether AAV-mediated restoration of MATR3 normalizes the Ddhd1/E2f4 module and prevents progressive neurite degeneration in primary cortical cultures.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NINDS/NIA RF1 and R01 multi-PI programs on distinct RNA-binding protein (MATR3 versus TDP-43/FUS liability states and splicing targets in ALS/FTD pathogenesis".

finding_title: Apc loss activates canonical Wnt feedback in Prkcd/Grin2c thalamic neurons
main_reason: Confidence is moderate (3) based on textbook canonical Wnt/beta-catenin destruction complex biochemistry. Novelty is low (2) because APC scaffolding function in beta-catenin degradation and downstream Wnt feedback induction (Axin2, Nkd1, Notum) is classic biology. The finding serves primarily as a robust positive control while mapping cell-type-specific thalamic metabolic (Gls) and amyloidogenic (Bace2) outputs. Support is sound and well grounded (4) with outstanding statistical signatures in 151 TH neurons (Axin2 log2FC +1.25, FDR 2.43e-16; Nkd1 log2FC +2.45, FDR 2.14e-13; Bace2 log2FC +2.29, FDR 1.30e-10; Gls log2FC -0.50, FDR 1.17e-12), though unmeasured beta-catenin nuclear translocation or TCF4/LEF1 chromatin binding. Priority is moderate (3) as it provides a reliable positive control for the in vivo perturbation platform, with focused follow-up potential for Wnt-mediated regulation of neuronal glutamate metabolism and BACE2 processing.
excited_community:
Canonical Wnt signaling laboratories, adult neuronal synapse remodeling groups, and subcortical neurobiology researchers.

Key Researchers and Laboratories:
a. Dr. Roeland Nurse (Stanford University School of Medicine) - discovery of Wnt signaling pathways, destruction complex regulation, and canonical target genes.
b. Dr. Hans Clevers (Hubrecht Institute) - Wnt target gene dynamics (Axin2, Nkd1) and destruction complex mechanics.
c. Dr. Patricia Salinas (University College London) - Wnt signaling in adult neuronal synapse maintenance, structural remodeling, and disease.
followup_programs:
Immediate Bench Experiments: Perform Western blotting and subcellular fractionation to quantify unphosphorylated active beta-catenin accumulation in the nuclear fraction of Apc-deficient thalamic neurons. Conduct CUT and RUN for beta-catenin and TCF4/LEF1 in thalamic neurons to confirm direct chromatin binding at promoter regions of Axin2, Nkd1, Notum, and Bace2. Measure intracellular glutamate and glutamine levels via LC-MS/MS to evaluate the functional metabolic impact of Gls (glutaminase) downregulation. Perform immunofluorescence for BACE2 and fluorometric beta-secretase activity assays to determine if Wnt activation accelerates APP cleavage in adult neurons. Conduct electrophysiological recordings of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in thalamic slices to evaluate synaptic remodeling following chronic Wnt/beta-catenin activation.

Grant-Funded Research Programs: NINDS/NIA research grants investigating postmitotic Wnt/Beta-catenin destruction complex signaling, thalamic glutamate metabolism, and synaptic maintenance.

finding_title: U2af2 perturbation depresses spliceosomal and calcium-handling genes in thalamic and midbrain neurons
main_reason: The response seems real becuase the gene counts are large and repeats in three classes, however the interpretation does not follow. The down list is dominated by Rsrp1, Srrm2, Luc7l2 and Srsf11, which are SR-rich transcripts whose levels are set by unproductive splicing and intron retention, so they fall after any spliceosome disruption. The synaptic homeostasis claim depends on Atp2a2 at -0.47 and Agrn at -0.56. No U2af2 self-transcript row is shown either, and the finding admits the assay cannot separate isoform switching from total mRNA change.
excited_community: U2AF65 is widely studied in cancer biology though. Some neurodevelopmental disorder genetics groups are studying U2AF2 patients with epilepsy. I am not sure.
followup_programs: The most promising experiment is to verify U2af2 knockdown and protein loss followed by running splicing-aware sequencing, because a count-based assay does not measure a 3-prime splice site factor. Also, confirm ATP2A2 at protein level and measure calcium handling.

finding_title: PPP2R1A perturbation reverses sterol-transcription polarity across neuronal classes
main_reason: The up arm is Msmo1, Insig1, Dhcr24 and Sc5d, while the down arm is Srebf2 and Hmgcr, so two different gene sets are grouped into one pathway and read as a reversal. There are predictable results because it is found that PP2A promotes SREBP-2 binding at the LDLR promoter after cholesterol depletion  and type-2A phosphatases activate HMG-CoA reductase in liver .
excited_community: DeBose-Boyd lab at UT Southwestern , TX works on SREBP and sterol regulation and could find this interesting.
followup_programs: The most important follow up experiment would be to test the same genes in both directions first because a reversal claim needs one gene flipping sign between classes at matched power. Since the mechanism is phosphorylation based, next step is to confirm PPP2R1A protein loss and measure PP2A activity, SREBP-2 cleavage and nuclear SREBP-2.

finding_title: YLPM1 perturbation lowers Srsf6-Srsf5 and Inha in midbrain-linked neurons
main_reason: The claim comes from one cell class only, and the genes that support it sit close to the significance cut-off. Srsf5 has FDR 0.00429 and Inha 0.0232, with effect sizes near -0.5 log2FC, so both calls could drop out if normalisation or cell filtering changes. That class, 155 MB Glut, also had the most perturbed cells, so its extra sensitivity alone may explain why the signal appears there. In the other classes only Ylpm1 itself moved, so the Srsf6 and Srsf5 part was never reproduced. The link to SR proteins was already plausible from published interactions of ZAP3 with Sam68, hnRNP-G and the NF110/NF45 dimer. Inha in neurons is an unusual and needs an expression sanity check.
excited_community: Computational work on YLPM1  is done at Mount Sinai in Mayan Lab. If phenotype is established, RNA processing groups in neuroscience will be interested.
followup_programs: The most promising  experiment would be to confirm YLPM1 protein loss because a 0.65 log2FC RNA drop can leave most protein intact for a 240 kDa scaffold.  Also, YLPM1 immunoprecipitation with mass spectrometry in neurons would show whether the PP1, SAM68 and hnRNP-G complex exists in this cell type as a secondary validation.

finding_title: Tpr loss induces a nuclear-transport transcriptional program centered on Ranbp6 and Xpo1
main_reason: The up arm is fits the interpretation, since Ranbp6 and Xpo1 are transport factors and their induction fits a transport stress response. But there is No Tpr self-transcript row is shown. A 5,087-gene response across 10 classes looks like a global collapse, and no viability or nuclear QC data is given. Priority stays high  becuase XPO1 is already a drug target in this disease area, because SINE compounds suppress transport deficits and neurodegeneration in a Drosophila C9-ALS model and improve neuron survival in TDP-43 rats.
excited_community: Nucleocytoplasmic transport and ALS groups would be interested in this research. The  Kielkopf lab at The University of Rochester Lab would be interested as the group is focused on the structural biology of pre-mRNA splicing including ALS.
followup_programs: The most promising experiments would be to first show TPR protein loss and measure mRNA export directly, with an oligo-dT FISH nuclear retention assay. Then add viability and nuclear QC metrics to check if the response is not from dying nuclei. Finally, test whether Xpo1 and Ranbp6 induction is protective or harmful by combining Tpr loss with a SINE compound or with Xpo1 knockdown. The ALS association would be interested to fund such research.

finding_title: ADNP perturbation defines a CHD4-adjacent neuronal signature across thalamic, midbrain, caudal GABAergic, and Pvalb populations
main_reason: Given markers shows different expression through sections so it is mostly single hits, except for Cacnb3 induction in two classes. The core idea names Cacnb3, Plppr3 and Atp9a, while the evidence rows for 151 are Xylt2, Cpne7 and Vstm2l, and 052 Pvalb Gaba contributes one FDR gene. Also the CHD4 has no occupancy data. ADNP with CHD4 in the ChAHP complex exactly is already established. Recurrent Cacnb3 induction in two classes could be tested epilepsy related syndrome.
excited_community: There is a dedicated ADNP Kids Research Foundation which supports researchers working on these projects. Dr. Kyle Fink at US Davis has several research papers on this and would be interested.
followup_programs: The most promising experiments on this would be ADNP and CHD4 CUT&RUN in the same mature neuron classes to test occupancy. Also confirm ADNP protein loss on orthogobal assays and then CACNB3 at protein level. A knock-in containing common patient-variant and snRNA-seq would show whether these markers are good for disease allele or just full knockdown.

finding_title: AP2M1 and AP2S1 perturbations converge on TFRC induction and sterol repression while AP2S1 adds cortical activity-gene loss
main_reason: Both self-transcripts fall with strong FDR, two physical subunits converge on the same genes, and Tfrc induction repeats in two classes for both. This makes it a good functional check that the perturbation worked. Also , the Tfrc arm is expected since AP-2 drives transferrin receptor uptake and the AP2M1 disease variant impairs it. Iron deficiency suppressing sterol synthesis would fit, and is testable to the Tfrc arm. The cortical Egr3, Arc, Bdnf and Vgf loss is expected from reduced vesicle recycling and lower activity.
excited_community: Synaptic endocytosis research groups, P2M1 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy clinical groups would be interested in this. I am not aware of any particular labs.
followup_programs: The most promising experiments would be to calculate surface TFRC, transferrin uptake and cellular iron in the same neurons. Then test the iron and sterol link directly by supplementing iron and check whether Srebf2 and Dhcr24 recovers and measure cholesterol content and SREBP-2 cleavage to verify at protein level.

finding_title: PGK1 and GAPDH perturbations converge on OGT and nuclear-speckle transcript loss
main_reason: PGK1, GADPH, and Tpi1 were perturbed in a large scale In-vivo CRISPR screen, revealing changes in the expression profiles of several genes including Ogt and Pnisr/Rsrp1 in hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons. These results suggest that perturbing these genes lead to a loss of OGT and nuclear speckle transcripts, as these effects are statistically robust (i.e. low DR values) they likely represent real biological phenomenon. However, given that the reported effect sizes are relatively small, I rated this finding as a 3 for both support and priority. This is because additional validation would be required to ensure these results are actually due to the perturbed genes and not just something like generic cellular stress.
excited_community: These data would be highly interesting to several neuroscience researchers. For example, researchers studying the biology of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease would be highly interested in these data given that  PGK1 and GAPDH are thought to be involved in the pathology of these conditions. More specifically, labs like the group of Timothy Ryan, who has studies PGK1 in the context of Parkinson's Disease Ryan at Cornell would likely be interested in these findings.
followup_programs: Several promising research programs could be built to follow up on these data. For example, if this were my project I would first validate these results by measuring the  OGT, PNISR, and RSRP1 levels in primary glutaminergic neurons where PGK1 and GADPH have been knocked down using shRNA. Once validated, microscopy studies could be performed to study/characterize changes in nuclear speckle morphology in response to the knockdown of  PGK1 and GAPDH. To fund this work investigators could apply for grants  from NIH institutes such as the NINDS (R01 grant) as this institute is known to fund basic neuroscience research. They could also apply for funding from private agencies such as the Michael J. Fox foundation as they are known to fund basic research relevant to Parkinson's disease.

finding_title: BMAL1-CLOCK and REV-ERB perturbations recover an asymmetric neuronal circadian feedback loop
main_reason: Proteins associated with the mammalian circadian clock were perturbed and the patterns that were discovered are consistent with previously reported findings. For example, the relationship between CLOCK and BMAL1 was confirmed via a quick google search. However, these data are useful in that they inspire confidence in the previously reported findings. In my opinion, they should also be followed up with moderate priority as dissecting these findings could help to further our understanding of the mammalian circadian clock.
excited_community: I would expect neuroscientists and researchers that are interested in studying the mammalian circadian rhythm to be interested in these data. For example, the groups of Joseph Takashi at UT Southwestern as well as the group of Erik Herzog at Washington University in St. Louis would be interested in these findings provided that they are validated.
followup_programs: I would be interested in examining how perturbing these genes affects the functional phenotypes of these neurons. For example, I would characterize these phenotypes when the circadian clock is disrupted. For example, I would perform assays to measure how the perturbed neurons respond to various neurotransmitters as well as to characterize the electrophysiology of the transfected neurons (patch clamp assays on brain slices containing the perturbed gene(s)). These findings could form the basis of an R01 grant or a funding application to a private foundation. Several public institutions (like the NINDS which funds basic neuroscience research) and private groups (like the Chan Zuckerberg initiative which have historically funded single cell transcriptomic studies) fund this kind of work. Researchers could approach these bodies to request financial support once supporting data are in place.

finding_title: STXBP1 perturbation produces distinct cortical, midbrain, and Pvalb transcriptional outputs
main_reason: Perturbation of STXBP1 led to distinct transcriptional changes in the cortex, midbrain, and Pvalb. Given extremely low FDR values these changes appear to be the result of real biological phenomena and not the result of chance. Furthermore, a quick google search suggests that these kinds of changes are previously unreported. Given the relevance of STXBP1 to several neurological disorders (STXBP1 Encephalopathy, epilepsy, etc.) these findings should be followed up with moderate priority.
excited_community: Neuroscientists, especially those that work on the biology of STXB1 and STXB1 related disorders would be highly interested in these data. This includes the groups of researchers such a Mingshan Xue at Baylor College of Medicine, and Dr. Jacqueline Burre at Cornell.
followup_programs: If I was responsible for this project, I would want to isolate the individual types of neurons metioned, knockdown STXB1, and perform western blots to validate the findings. Once the findings are validated, experiments could be performed to characterize the underlying physiology of these neurons. For example, given that STXBP1 is known to regulate the SNARE complex which is involved in neurotransmitter release it would be interesting to perform functional assays to study the impacts of the reported gene expression changes on this process. Several funding agencies would be interested in funding this work if these data were validated. These include public agencies like the NINDS which funds basic neurobiology work as well as private agencies like the STXB1 foundation (as they actively fund research into the biology of STXB1).

finding_title: PPP2R1A perturbation defines a cortical Amy1-high, Rsrp1/Leng8-low reporter state with TSC/STXBP1 neighborhood structure
main_reason: PPP2R1A perturbation led to an upregulation of Amy1, Rnpc3, Stmn4, Jun, Pcsk1n, Ovgp1 while simultneously leading to repression of Rsrp1, Leng8, Kifc2, and Pabpn1. Based on a quick literature search, this appears to have been previously unreported suggesting that these findings may be novel (however, I cannot assess this with certainty as I am not experienced in this field). Given that these findings are not due to chance (low FDR values) and that PPP2R1A has been linked to neurological disorders (PPP2R1A-related neurodevelopmental disorder) these findings should be followed up with moderate priority as they could lead to new insights into neurobiology and nerodegenerative diseases.
excited_community: Several groups of neuroscientists would be interested in these findings. Specifically, these data would be especially relevant to scientists studying Jordan's syndrome and Houge-Janssens syndrome as PPP2R1A mutations have been linked to both of these disorders. These include groups like the the groups of Wendy Chung at Boston Children's hospital which known for studying the biology of Jordan's syndrome.
followup_programs: In my opinion, a promising research program would use these data to examine the variants of PPP2R1A that are associated with genetic disorders to see if these variants correspond to the transcriptional profile that was revealed in the perturbation experiment. If so, this could enable further research where these signals act a baseline for PPP2R1A dysfunction. Further research could also focus on other types of neurons to see if the effects are cell specific or if the discovered transcriptional signature also applies more generally to other neuronal cell types. Many grants from both public and private sources are available for this kind of research. This includes grants from public institutes such as the NINDS (R01) and grants from private foundations like Jordan's Guardian angels (an organization that funds Jordan's syndrome research). Given that the NINDS funds basic neuroscience research while Jordan's guardian angels is interested in studying Jordan's syndrome (in which PPP2R1A has been implicated) these funding organizations are highly relevant.

finding_title: Rnpc3 loss creates a core spliceosome response centered on Mapk8, Ap2a1, Wdfy1, Pcyt2, and Pten
main_reason: These data suggest that a perturbation of Rnpc3 has an effect on genes such as Mapk8, Ap2a1, Wdfy1, Pcyt2, and Pten. This suggests that perturbing the spliceosome has an effect on these genes which, based on a brief internet search, seems to be unreported. Therefore, these findings appear novel, and may be relevant to diseases that are associated with Rnpc3 such as Roifman syndrome. Given this and the fact that the FDR values are very small, these effects are likely not due to chance and these data should be followed up with moderate priority.
excited_community: Neuroscientists studying Rnpc3 or scientists studying general mRNA splicing mechanisms in neurons and their relevance to disease would be highly interested in these data. For example, the lab of Douglas Black at UCLA studies mRNA splicing in neurons and might be interested in these data.
followup_programs: If this were my project I would perform a number of experiments including characterizing and verifying the effects of the Rnpc3 perturbation on mRNA splicing via long read seuqencing (i.e. oxford nanopore). I would also verify that the genes whose transcription profiles are modified when Rnpc3 is perturbed also translate into differences in the expression of the respective proteins. Specifically, I would confirm this via western blotting. Once this is verified, these findings could be used as the basis to support a novel research program. This program could be supported by grants from groups such as the NINDS which funds basic neurobiology work or private groups like the Chang Zuckerberg foundation (which has been known to fund transcriptomics projects in the context of neurobiology).

finding_title: Kansl1 loss perturbs midbrain lysosomal and Golgi trafficking transcripts
main_reason: These data suggest that perturbation of Kansl1 leads to significant changes in several lysosomal and Golgi trafficking transcripts in the midbrain. Given that the effects are somewhat large and the FDR values are low these effects appear to be due to real biological phenomena rather than chance. Furthermore,  as Kansl1 is involved in the neurological disorder known as Koolen-de Vries syndrome, these data should be followed up with moderate priority as they could provide insights into the condition. However, I am unable to assess novelty as I have limited experience in this field.
excited_community: Neuroscientists that study lysosomal and golgi traficking as well as those who study Koolen-de Vries syndrome would be highly interested in these data. For example, the lab of Dr. Hellen Willsey at UCSF is involved in Koolen-de Vries syndrome research and would likely be interested in these data.
followup_programs: If I was leading this project, I would be interested in Isolating primary neurons, knocking down Kansl1 using shRNA, and then using RNA seq to validate the effects of the perturbation on the reported genes. If validated, I would then suggest performing live cell imaging assays to assess effects of the knockdown on phagosome/lysosome fusion and golgi/ER trafficking. However, as I am not a neuroscientist I am not able to suggest the specific proteins to tag without significant online research that would be beyond the scope of this survey. With regards to funding agencies, this research program could be supported by R01 grants from public institutions like the NINDS (funds basic neurobiology research) or by grants from private organizations like the Koolen-de Vries Syndrome (KVDS) Foundation (provides grants to support research into KVDS).

finding_title: Acute TBR1 perturbation recurrently raises CPNE6 while splitting mature cortical projection-neuron outputs
main_reason:
TBR1 is a known transcription repressor gene and is associated with autism. So this is a known functional gene towards the neurodegeneration disease. Among all affected genes, the recurrent CPNE6 gene is associated with synaptic transmission(PMID: 29802203); and the CACNA1G is associated with neurodegeneration disease (spinocerebellar). 

Novelty: Because the recurrent CPNE6-center is associated with neuro function, the novelty is discounted. 

Support: The supporting evidence is well ground because CPNE6 is recurrent from two perturbations and the FDR is significant.
excited_community: Chen Bin from UC Santa Cruze who is studying the TBR1 function on the neuronal identity and connectivity
followup_programs:
Since TBR1 is a transcription factor and there are so many targets here. The first thing is to perform a ChiP-Seq to distinguish direct and indirect targets, such as CPNE6 and CACNA1G. 

Since this is still an exploratory research on the TBR1 target, this can fit to a NIH R21 grant that designed for Exploratory/Developmental grants (R21).

finding_title: Distinct endomembrane perturbations converge on a proteostasis-associated neighborhood with node-specific outputs
main_reason:
Novelty: It is novel to perturb the endomembrane related genes and test their function in neuro cells as the majority of those studies are not performed in neuro cells. Although lots of perturbed genes are metabolic genes, many of them are already also associated with neurodegeneration disease: ATP6V0C is associated with seizure (ClinVar); CAMLG is associated with Parkinson Disease (PMID: 40053464); as well as PI4KA (ClinVar) and VPS53 (ClinVar). 

Support: It is well supported with many neurodegeneration related genes : ATP6V0A1 (ClinVar, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy); and SLC12A5 (malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy). Combining all that evidence, this is a very high priority experiment due to several associated genes and convergent function to neurodegeneration disease.
excited_community: Andreas Ernst, from UCSD who is studying cryo-EM of protein condensates in the early secretory pathway of neurons.
followup_programs:
Experiments: Since many genes here are associated with neurodegeneration disease, it is suggested to do a global mass spectrometry proteomics to validate the protein-level with the same trends with expression level. If true, this can be extended to a knock down mice model for phenotypic observations. 

Grant-fund: this can fit into a NIH R01 for a very comprehensive proposal for studying the function of endomembrane in neuro cells.

finding_title: Zbtb11 perturbation recurrently lowers Rbm28, Stx16, Acsf3, and Ndufaf1 across subcortical neurons
main_reason:
ZBTB11 is a transcription factor that regulates the transcription process. It is reported to be associated with intellectual developmental disorder (ClinVar). 

Novelty: The affected genes are mostly not relevant with neurodegeneration disease, making this a potential new mechanism for ZBTB11 function. And the genes of ACSF3, RBM28, and STX16 are associated with genetic disease that do not belong to neurodegeneration disease. So this study may point to a new mechanism of ZBTB11 with high novelty. 

Support: The core signals of RBM28, STX16, and ACSF3 are recurrent from many perturbations with a significant FDR. So the support is also very high.
excited_community: Doriana Misceo from Olso University who is studying the genetics of ZBTB11 variants and spectrum on several diseases.
followup_programs:
CHIP-Seq to test whether transcription factor ZBTB11 directly binds to the promoter or enhancer regions of those non-mitochondrial genes like RBM28, STX16 (ACSF3 is mitochondrial related).

This can trigger a NIH R21 Exploratory/Developmental grant to define this potential new mechanism for ZBTB11.

finding_title: Rab7 loss elicits a lysosomal hydrolase and sterol-response state
main_reason:
Novelty: 1) the result convergent to lysosome biogenesis genes (ATP6V1B2, ATP6V0B, LAMP2, MCOLN1), providing future druggable opportunity. 2) Preciously define the signals for RAB7 perturbation in neuro cells. All those are new results with no previous publications.


Support: All signals are very significant with extremely low FDR, and the genes can be convergent to specific pathways. The overall evidence is well ground.
excited_community: Chonglin Yang from Yunnan University who is studying the Rab7 effect on the mice neuro cells through the lysosome function.
followup_programs:
Promising experiment: conduct a scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq across different thalamic vs. mid brain after the RAB7 perturbation. This will help to evaluate the chromatic accessibility difference in two types of tissues for their lysosome genes specifically: ATP6V1B2, ATP6V0B, LAMP2, MCOLN1. 

This can fit to a grant by the National Institute of Aging with focus on Lysosomal dysfunction.

finding_title: Ogt loss represses RNA-processing and cholesterol-turnover transcripts while relieving Xpo1
main_reason:
Novelty: both OGA and OGT are post-translation genes. The perturbation caused by genes of RNA homeostasis are not expected and not reported (Rsrp1/Xpo1). This may extend OGA/OGT function to RNA processing role in the neuro cells.

Support: the genes are convergent to either spliceosome related genes (RSRP1, SRRM2) or RNA transportation related genes (XPO1). The evidence FDR is also very significant. The evidence is well grounded.
excited_community: Christina M. Woo from Harvard University who is studying the O-GlcNAc homeostasis with small molecular
followup_programs:
Promising experiments: try a Ribo-Seq after Ogt knockdown to test whether this will affect the global expression pattern change through the spliceosomal dysfunction on RsRP1, SRRM2. This can help to better understand the effect of Ogt knockdown. 

Research program: this can be a proof-of-concept grant that fits NIH R21 Exploratory grant, with a future extension to R01 grant to study the mechanism of Ogt control RNA homeostasis.

finding_title: HSPA8 perturbation induces a compact HSP70-HSP90 compensatory transcript arm
main_reason:
HSPA8 is a molecular chaperone implicated in a wide variety of cellular processes. Among all affected genes, DNAJA1, HSPA4L, HSP90AA1, HSPH1, DNAJB1 are all protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (hsa04141). 

Novelty: It is possible to expect the compensation effect within the chaperone. After google search, there is no specific definition in the neuro cell line with so many target genes. So this is apparently unreported and non-obvious. 

Support: All the FDR are significant, but in a range of 0.01-1E-4. Most genes are chaperone related, and have no potential target for neurodegeneration disease. So the support for future exploration on neurodegeneration disease is not that high.
excited_community: Kenneth Fischbach from National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, who is studying the mechanism of neurological disease: protein quality control by HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA8 complex.
followup_programs:
Experiments: Single Cell ATAC-seq to decide whether HSPA8 perturbation has any chromatic accessibility changes on the chaperone genes, this will help to confirm HSPA8 did change the overall pattern of chaperon gene expression. 

Program: this can fit into a NIH R21 Exploratory/Developmental Grant to define the global multi-omics pattern of HSPA8 perturbation.

finding_title: PPP3CA and PPP3R1 perturbations expose a noncanonical calcineurin transcript output opposite AP-2 adaptor states
main_reason: The data support distinct transcriptional responses to Ppp3ca and Ppp3r1 perturbation, with some connection to genes involved in calcium and synaptic function. I do not have direct experience with calcineurin or synaptic endocytosis, but I do have experience with gene perturbation and transcriptomic analysis, so I have moderate confidence in my evaluation. I scored the support as moderate because both target genes were significantly depleted, but the proposed connection to AP-2 is based on anticorrelated expression signatures rather than functional interaction or epistasis. The finding is moderately novel and worth following up, but it seems much of the underlying calcineurin and endocytosis biology is already established
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from researchers studying calcineurin signaling, synaptic vesicle recycling, neuronal calcium signaling, and synaptic plasticity. Groups studying calcineurin-dependent neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders could also be interested. One such lab is the Isabelle Mansuy Lab (University of Zurich / ETH Zurich) who studies calcineurin's role in the brain.
followup_programs: I would first validate the Ppp3ca/Ppp3r1 transcriptional signatures and test whether pertubation actually changes NFAT activity, calcium signaling or AP to dependent endocytosis. Double perturbation of calcineurin and a P2 components would be especially useful for determining whether the opposing RNA signatures represent a functional relationship rather than antic correlation. It validated this could fit with NINDS or NIMH funding focused on synaptic signaling and neuronal function.

finding_title: Wdr26 loss produces a cerebellar GABA channel-and-splicing signature
main_reason: The transcriptional response is large, and several of the strongest changes are supported by very low FDRs, with Srrm2 repression also recurring in midbrain and posterior GABAergic neurons. I do not have direct experience with WDR26 or cerebellar biology, but I do have experience with gene perturbation, transcriptomics, and RNA processing, so I have moderate confidence in my evaluation. I scored the support highly because the response is strong and includes recurrent effects, although the proposed CTLH/GID mechanism and cerebellar specificity are not directly demonstrated. I assigned high priority because linking WDR26 loss to RNA-processing and neuronal excitability genes could provide a new mechanism to investigate in Skraban-Deardorff syndrome.
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from Skraban-Deardorff syndrome and WDR26 laboratories, as well as researchers studying CTLH/GID ubiquitin ligases, cerebellar inhibitory neurons, RNA processing, and neurodevelopmental disorders.
followup_programs: I would prioritize validating the channel and splicing changes, particularly Srrm2, Cacna1g, and Grik1, and then use RNA-seq capable of measuring alternative splicing to determine whether loss of splicing-factor transcripts produces actual splicing defects. Electrophysiology could test whether the channel changes alter cerebellar GABA-neuron excitability. This could be a good fit for NINDS/NICHD neurodevelopmental-disease funding and rare-disease funding focused on Skraban-Deardorff syndrome.

finding_title: Thap11 perturbation reveals a conserved Rabac1-Sdccag8-Gdap1 mitochondrial/ciliary module
main_reason: The transcriptional response is strong and includes the same small set of genes across several neuronal populations, which makes the underlying signal convincing. I do not have direct experience with THAP11, cilia, or mitochondrial quality-control biology, but I do have experience with gene perturbation and transcriptomic analysis, so I have moderate confidence in my evaluation. I scored the support highly because the changes are large, statistically strong, and recurrent, although the data do not establish that these genes are direct THAP11 targets or that they form a functional cilia/mitochondria module. I assigned high priority because the recurrent signature appears relatively unexpected and could identify a new role for THAP11 in mature neurons.
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from researchers studying THAP11 and transcriptional regulation, as well as groups working on ciliopathies, mitochondrial biology, and neuronal quality control. Researchers studying SDCCAG8, GDAP1, or PRKN-associated neurological disease may also be interested.
followup_programs: I would first reproduce the transcriptional signature and use THAP11 occupancy assays such as CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq to determine whether the recurrent genes are direct targets. Functional studies of mitochondrial activity and ciliary structure would then test whether the transcriptional signature corresponds to the proposed biology. If validated, this could fit NINDS-funded work on neuronal mitochondrial function, ciliopathies, and neurodevelopmental disease.

finding_title: Arid1a, Smarcb1, Smarcc2, and Smarce1 perturbations converge on Ptpn3-Reep2-Prkcd repression with Clstn2-Nexn induction
main_reason: The convergence of four BAF subunit perturbations on the same transcriptional signature provides strong support for a shared regulatory program. Because chromatin remodeling is related to, but not within, my primary area of expertise, I have moderate confidence in the evaluation. I scored the support highly because the same genes changed in the same direction across multiple perturbation with strong statistical significance, although protein depletion and BAF occupancy were not measured. I assigned this finding high priority because, if validated, it would improve our understanding of mature neural BAF complex function and have implications forSWI/SNF-associated neurodevelopmental disorders such as Coffin-Siris syndrome.
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from research or studying SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin remodeling, neuronal chromatin regulation, and transcriptional control of neuronal identity. Finding would also be relevant to laboratories investigating Coffin-Siris and other SWI/SNF-associated neural developmental disorders, as well as researcher studying how BAF complex composition changes between neuronal development and maturity. Such laboratories might include the Crabtree laboratory (Stanford University) and the Kadoch laboratory (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute) which investigate BAF complex biology and its role in development and disease.
followup_programs: I would first determine whether the shared transcriptional signature reflects direct BAF complex occupancy using chromatin accessibility and chromatin binding assays and confirm comparable protein depletion across the different BAF subunit perturbations. I would then test whether the affected transcriptional program is reversible in mature neurons and whether different subunits are functionally redundant after neuronal differentiation. This work could support and NINDS and NICHD funded research programs investigating neuronal chromatin remodeling, SWI/SNF complex function, and molecular basis of Coffin-Siris and related neurodevelopmental disorders.

finding_title: Ranbp2 perturbation produces Srrm2-down/Rbm15-up cortical and Grm1-Epha4-Itpr1-up cerebellar responses
main_reason: The data support different transcriptional responses to Ranbp2 perturbation in cortical and cerebellar neurons, but each response is based on only a few significant genes with relatively modest FDRs. I do not have direct experience with RANBP2, nuclear transport, or SUMOylation, but I do have experience with RNA processing, gene perturbation, and transcriptomic analysis, so I have moderate confidence in my evaluation. I scored the support conservatively because the proposed two-branch mechanism is based on different gene sets in two neuronal populations, and SUMOylation, nuclear transport, and calcium signaling were not measured. The cell-type-dependent response is interesting and relatively unexpected, but the limited evidence makes this a moderate rather than high priority.
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from researchers studying RANBP2, nuclear-pore biology, SUMOylation, and neuronal nuclear transport. The Srrm2/Rbm15 response could also interest RNA-processing groups, while the cerebellar response may be relevant to researchers studying calcium signaling and cerebellar neuronal function.
followup_programs: I would first reproduce the cortical and cerebellar transcriptional responses and confirm RANBP2 protein loss. Measuring nuclear transport and SUMOylation would test the proposed upstream mechanism, while splicing analysis in cortical neurons and calcium measurements in cerebellar neurons could determine whether the two transcriptional signatures correspond to functional changes. If validated, this could support NINDS-funded work on nuclear-pore dysfunction and neuron-specific mechanisms of neurological disease.

finding_title: KLF9 perturbation defines a Wsb1/Rasgrp2/Pld3 thalamic module distinct from KLF7 and KLF13 outputs
main_reason: The data identify a small KLF9-associated transcriptional signature, but the finding is based on only 19 significant genes in one neuronal population. I do not have direct experience with KLF9 biology, but I do have experience with gene perturbation and transcriptomic analysis, so I have moderate confidence in my evaluation. I scored the support low because Klf9 itself was not significantly depleted and the apparent differences from KLF7 and KLF13 could reflect unequal perturbation rather than true paralog-specific biology. Although the specific marker combination is new, KLF paralogs were already expected to have distinct neuronal functions, making this a low-priority finding without additional validation.
excited_community: I would expect the strongest interest from researchers studying KLF transcription factors, thyroid hormone signaling, and neuronal maturation. Groups investigating transcriptional regulation of mature thalamic neurons may also be interested if the KLF9-specific response is validated.
followup_programs: I would first confirm effective KLF9 perturbation and determine whether the Wsb1/Rasgrp2/Pld3 response is reproducible. Comparing KLF9, KLF7, and KLF13 perturbations under matched conditions would help establish whether the differences are truly paralog-specific. Given the limited evidence, I would prioritize validation before pursuing substantial funding, although a confirmed mechanism could fit NINDS-funded research on transcriptional regulation and neuronal maturation.

finding_title: NatB catalytic-subunit loss represses a Peg3-Kifc2-Snhg11 program in many neurons
main_reason: Based on the available literature surrounding Naa20 and NatB, there were no reported studies that associate the loss of NatB with repression of the RNA program that includes Peg3-Kifc2-Snhg11 across neurons. The gene perturbation data is impressive due to the vast number of cell classes evaluated which mostly indicate recurrent same-direction hits for genes Peg3, Kifc2 and Snhg11, however gene perturbation data by itself is insufficient in making this finding higher than moderate priority; elucidating the specific NatB substrate would do well to add confidence to the claim and increase the priority of this study.
excited_community: Ophir Shalem from Department of Genetics, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA would be a great potential researcher. Ophir recently published an article (PMID: 38335281) regarding NatB inhibition as a therapeutic avenue for lowering alpha-synuclein levels which correlate with Parkinsons and related neurodegenerative diseases. Since this finding uncovered specific RNA programs that are recurrently repressed upon NatB perturbation, perhaps Ophir's lab would be interested in doing a deep-dive on the findings of this study for uncovering the mechanistic basis of NatB inhibition-associated reduction of alpha synuclein.
followup_programs: I would highly recommend performing an N-terminal proteomics study where wild-type cells with an intact Naa20 are compared against a cell line with Naa20 knockout and identifying mass spec shifts to elucidate potential substrates that cause the recurrent RNA programs. This experiment would make the study more mechanistic and overall stronger in its claims. For funding programs, I would recommend: The Michael J. Fox Foundation Pipeline due to its focus on Parkinson's disease. As stated from PMID: 38335281, NatB inhibition may help attenuate alpha synuclein, which is attributed to neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson's making this program a great fit for the finding.

finding_title: Acute Tsc1 and Tsc2 loss couples mTOR derepression to a sterol-lysosome module in postnatal neurons
main_reason: The finding does not display a high novelty value as previous reports have shown already that Tsc loss can lead to lysosomal biogenesis (PMID: 34253722) and cholesterol homeostasis (PMID: 28498820). The supporting data is plausible however, showing in mature neurons, a strong consistent overlap of induced lysosomal biogenesis and cholesterol homeostasis genes in 155 MB Glut, Tsc1 and Tsc2 in the same cell class, however gene expression by itself could be strengthened by providing results on phenotype related to lysosomal biogenesis and cholesterol homeostasis as a result of Tsc1 and Tsc2 perturbation; considering the low novelty and plausible supporting data, this finding is low priority.
excited_community: For an interested researcher, I would recommend Elizabeth P Henske from the Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA who studied both lysosomal biogenesis and cholesterol homeostasis related to TSC loss. The two studies from this lab delve more into mechanistic underlying basis of how TSC loss can contribute to lysosomal biogenesis and cholesterol homeostasis. However the lab may be interested in investigating how mature neurons are associated with TSC regulation of these two pathways and may provide more insight on mechanisms making her a good fit for this finding.
followup_programs: I would suggest performing a colorimetric cholesterol assay after Tsc1 and Tsc2 perturbation to verify the phenotypes associated with TSC perturbation. Additionally, characterization of lysosomal membrane and staining can be performed using acid dyes to evaluate vesicle functionality in addition to immunofluorescence microscopy to examine if lysosomal area is affected. If both provide positive results in Tsc1/2 perturbation, this would help support the claims made by the finding. For grant and funding programs, I would suggest the Lysosomal Disease Network which funds specific research related to lysosomal-associated disorders; this could be a good fit since lysosomal biogenesis is one of the key pathways in this finding, or the American Heart Association which funds metabolic related research which ties into the findings focus on cholesterol homeostasis.

finding_title: ZMYM2 perturbation induces a Notum/Echdc2/F11r/Atp2a3 thalamic signature
main_reason: The finding seems to be unreported and non-obvious; there were no obvious reports that directly associate ZMYM2 perturbation with a Notum/Echdc2/F11r/Atp2a3 thalamic signature. While the data shows increased expression of Notum/Echdc2/F11r/Atp2a3 in 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut, the supporting data overall seems weak since Zmym2 transcript was not FDR-reduced which questions whether Zmym2 was efficiently perturbed and guide-specific effects are not able to be excluded; given the weak supporting data, this study falls under low priority.
excited_community: For interested researchers, Morgan Sheng from the Stanley Center for Psychiatric Research, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA USA would be a great fit for this finding. Morgan's recent publication (PMID: 41022686) studied Zmym2 due to its schizophrenia-associated risk. Specifically, Morgan evaluated mice with individual loss-of-function mutation of Zmym2 in the thalamus, similarly as done in the current finding. The author of the finding could find value in the data sets of Morgan's work that relate more to mechanistic-based insight regarding Zmym2 loss-of-function in the thalamus.
followup_programs: The first thing I would recommend to the user of this finding would be to re-validate the data and ensure that Zmym2 perturbation was efficiently performed and that guide-specific effects can be excluded through qPCR comparing wildtype vs perturbed Zmym2 and designing more than one gRNA targeting different exons of Zmym2. Doing so would provide a reliable dataset where more conclusions can be drawn and built upon. I would also recommend that meta-data analyses be performed to see if any datasets exist that show whether Zmym2 variants correlate with Notum and Atp2a3 changes in gene expression in thalamus. For funding opportunities, I would recommend the NIH National Institutes of Health R01 focused on chromatin regulation as Zmym2 is commonly associated with chromatin biology.

finding_title: Rb1 and E2f4 perturbations release distinct replication and chromosome-repair arms in thalamic neurons
main_reason: Rb1 and E2f4 are known to have related but distinct functions, and Rb1 and E2f4 knockouts or mutants have been studied in different cell types in a few different publications (PMID: 20023434, PMID:23077065, PMID:38637503), therefore, the supportive data where the expression changes for DNA duplication and chromosome repair upon Rb1 and E2f4 seem expected. In terms of the significance and novelty, a similar concept has been reported in which a dominant negative form of E2F4 acts as a multifactorial therapeutic agent for Alzheimer’s disease (PMID: 36292945), echoing the concept of selectively suppressing one arm to achieve therapeutic effects, therefor the finding seems to have weak significance and novelty.
excited_community: Jose Frade from the department of molecular, cellular and developmental neurobiology at Cajal Institute would be interested in this finding as his lab established transgenic mice as a tool for evaluating E2F4 as a therapeutic target in neuropathology and brain aging. Jose Frades may find value in this data set generated in thalamic neurons as it supports the possibility of E2F4 as a potential target and provides more insights from a different model for mechanism research.
followup_programs: RB1 and E2F4 protein levels upon perturbation should be measured using western blot and confirmed before evaluating downstream transcriptomic changes. I would recommend performing Rb1 and E2f4 perturbation in vivo (whole body and brain/neuron-specific) to test whether the mature neurons are protective with minimum side effects elsewhere to explore the safety of selective suppression of one arm to protect mature neurons. In terms of grant opportunity, National Institute on Aging (NIA) Notices of Funding Opportunity (NOFOs) - Novel Mechanism Research on Neuropsychiatric Symptoms (NPS) in Alzheimer's Dementia (R01 Clinical Trial Optional) may be a good fit, as RB1 and E2F4 dysregulation are associated with neurodegeneration, and this finding may further support a new direction for future therapeutic strategies.

finding_title: ACTB perturbation recurrently induces ACTG1 and FLNA without reciprocal ACTG1 compensation
main_reason: The finding appears to be under known biology in a substantially new context; although there are studies that evaluate mutations in Actb and Actg1 under de novo conditions (PMID: 22366783) causing Baraitser-Winter syndrome, no study was found where induction of Actg1/Flna as a result of Actb perturbation without ACTG1 compensation was uncovered. The supporting data gives plausibility for the finding demonstrating that at least 13/22 contexts and 9/22 contexts for Flna and Actg1 respectively increased after Actb perturbation, however protein level validation to merit a higher priority for this study.
excited_community: William B Dobyns from the Department of Pediatrics and Neurology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA would be a good fit for this finding. William has published a study regarding Actb and Actg1 de novo mutations examining exome sequencing data and the prominence of craniofacial appearances in patients. The exome sequencing datasets could be interesting for the author of the current finding and could follow up with the analysis of trends in Flna expression.
followup_programs: Promising experiments could include the evaluation of protein expressions to see whether the data aligns with gene expression performed through a western-blot of collected extracts containing disrupted ACTB and ACTG1; if the data aligns, this strengthens the confidence in the idea that ACTB perturbation leads to induction of ACTG1 and FLNA without reciprocal ACTG1 compensation . Furthermore, meta-data analyses from published data such as PMID: 22366783 could be useful to see if sequencing data similarly aligns with the results of the finding. Research programs that would fit well with this finding include National Science Foundation (NSF) under their biological science grants which includes cytoskeletal filament assembly. This fits in well with the finding as the study focuses on a cytoplasmic actin perturbation data.

finding_title: Tardbp and Fus perturbations create opposite Snrnp70 responses within separable recurrent RNA-processing states
main_reason: From my brief search of available literature, while it is known that TDP-43 is a repressor of cryptic exons in cell-type dependent RNA and FUS binds brain RNA and regulates alternative splicing, both Tardbp and Fus perturbations appear unprecedented in regards to contrasting responses in Snrnp70 in neuronal regions making this finding fall under known biology but in a substantially new context; the closes finding appeared to be relating to FUS domains involved in Snrnp70 regulation (PMID: 32915994). The supporting data is plausible given the consistent trends observed under Tardbp/Fus perturbation in 3 regions: 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut, 191 MB P MY GABA and 191 MB P MY GABA and 151 TH, 155 MB and 191 MB where Tardbp decreased Snrnp70 and Fus increased Snrnp70; however, the supporting data could be stronger by way of including protein level data.
excited_community: Tadashi Nakaya's group from the School of Pharmacy at Fukuoka, International University of Health and Welfare, Fukuoka, Japan would be a great fit for this finding. Tadashi made a recently publication regarding FUS domains that contributed to the regulation of Snrnp70 which relates to this finding through mutual interest of Fus-associated impacts on Snrnp70 expression.
followup_programs: I would recommend evaluating protein level trends in addition to RNA expression to prove that Snrnp70 response goes beyond the transcript and provide more context behind protein interaction. I would suggest performing a western blot in Fus/Tardbp perturbations of the specific subcellular regions to evaluate whether the proteins also follow the trends observed in perturbation assays in addition to Snrnp70. Since this finding relates to ALS-gene response, the American Brain Foundation would be a good possible fit for grant-funding as the program has historically funded ALS-centric research in addition to brain diseases and disorders.

finding_title: SP4 perturbation defines a Tsga10/Abhd11/Svip module in posterior glutamatergic neurons
main_reason:
SP4 is widely established as a GC/GT-box binding transcription factor involved in neurodevelopmental and NMDAR subunit regulation, such as Grin1 (Milagre, I., Nunes, M. J., Castro-Caldas, M., Moutinho, M., Gama, M. J., & Rodrigues, E. (2012). Neuronal differentiation alters the ratio of Sp transcription factors recruited to the CYP46A1 promoter. Journal of neurochemistry, 120(2), 220–229. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1471-4159.2011.07577.x). Its role in regulating this specific metabolic/organellar transcriptomic module isin adult posterior glutamatergic populations (155 MB Glut / 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut) has not been previously reported, to my knowledge. So, the proposed role of SP4 in driving a specific posterior glutamatergic program (Tsga10, Abhd11, Svip, Strada, Dnajc4) is novel. 
The evidence here is weak with perturbation directionality conflict, data annotation inconsistencies like data-labeling mix-up between cluster 155 and cluster 151, and lack of functional validation. So, this makes it low priority for follow-up research.

As this is a novel finding, there is no prior research work that supports or establishes this claim.
excited_community:
1. Ines Milagre, Research Institute for Medicines and Pharmaceutical Sciences (iMed.UL), University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal.
This researcher has worked on and published impactful data regarding SP4 (Milagre, I., Nunes, M. J., Castro-Caldas, M., Moutinho, M., Gama, M. J., & Rodrigues, E. (2012). Neuronal differentiation alters the ratio of Sp transcription factors recruited to the CYP46A1 promoter. Journal of neurochemistry, 120(2), 220–229. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1471-4159.2011.07577.x) and would be interested in this finding.

2. Xianjin Zhou, Department of Psychiatry, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA:

The most direct connection is with calcium channels, which are involved in the role of lysosomes as a calcium store. It is plausible that loss of V-ATPase in neurons also causes a downstream loss of calcium channels, but this must be disambiguated from the wider viability effect. The interpretation requires additional validation, as well as confirmation that effects are not viability-related and that cell type specificity is confirmed.

followup_programs: The priority is confirming the validity of the experiment, given that MAX RNA and protein did not match the expected loss. Further, the screen does not confirm that the finding is isolated to TH and MB, so these results should be checked in other tissue and cell types. The proposed branching model should be tested mechanistically, testing the role of MAX  and MGA binding partners in MYC and meiosis repression as well as the new potential branch of neuronal clock control. If the work has a cancer angle, the NCI would be the primary funder.

finding_title: GRIN2A raises an L2/3 NPTX2-BDNF-PTGS2 program while GRIN2B trends oppositely and significantly lowers Vgf and Kcnv1
main_reason:
I marked this as "known biology in a new context" because the genetically and functionally distinct roles of GRIN2A and GRIN2B variants in neurological disorders are already well established (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6871362/).
However, the claim that "GRIN2A raises an L2/3 NPTX2-BDNF-PTGS2 program while GRIN2B trends oppositely" is not adequately supported by the evidence presented in the Support section. The statistically supported data show that Grin2a perturbation significantly increased Nptx2, Bdnf, and Ptgs2. In contrast, although Grin2b perturbation moved Bdnf (−1.156, FDR 0.184), Nptx2 (−1.032, FDR 0.617), and Ptgs2 (−1.453, FDR 0.286) in the opposite direction, none of these changes reached FDR significance (<0.05). Therefore, the proposed opposite transcriptional program is based only on directional trends rather than statistically supported evidence. Furthermore, the authors acknowledge that Grin2a itself was not significantly depleted in L2/3 (log2FC −0.401, FDR 0.274), which further weakens the interpretation that the observed expression changes result from effective Grin2a loss.

Overall, the evidence does not sufficiently support the central claim, so I rated the data support as Unsound. Consequently, I also assigned this finding a Low Priority.
excited_community: Dr. Yan Wu. Beijing Key Laboratory of Neural Regeneration and Repair, Department of Anatomy, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Beijing Institute of Brain Disorders, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Their publication  (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8373273/) shows their interest in GRIN2A, Nptx2, Bdnf, and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
followup_programs:
The most promising simple experiment would be a qPCR validation in the same neuronal model after GRIN2A and GRIN2B perturbation. Check if Grin2a and Grin2b are actually reduced. The first step here is to verify that the perturbation was successful. Only then, it makes sense to interpret downstream changes in the marker genes.

Grant: Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI). Since GRIN2A and GRIN2B variants are implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism, (https://www.chop.edu/conditions-diseases/grin2a-related-disorders) this project could be a good fit for SFARI funding.

finding_title: HSF1 perturbation lowers a basal HSPH1-HSP90 support module
main_reason:
HSF1 is already known to regulate heat-shock proteins, as supported by the cited data. The new aspect that the data suggest is that HSF1 also maintains the baseline expression of chaperone proteins (HSPH1-HSP90) in neurons, even without heat stress. So this is a known biology in a new context, not a completely new mechanism. 
They did not confirm that HSF1 was effectively knocked down (As mentioned in the "Support" section: Hsf1 RNA itself was not significantly reduced), nor did they measure protein levels or chaperone function. Therefore, the conclusion is supported but not fully validated.
excited_community: Dr. Didier Picard. Département de Biologie Moléculaire et Cellulaire, Université de Genève, Genève, Switzerland. Their highly cited study (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10703448/) indicates their interest in HSP90, molecular chaperones, and HSF1-regulated protein homeostasis.
followup_programs: The most promising experiment, I think, would be to measure HSP90/HSPH1 protein levels after HSF1 perturbation by Western blot or immunostaining. The claim is that HSF1 maintains the basal chaperone module. The RNA data somewhat support this, but the study did not measure protein abundance. Confirming that HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and HSPH1 proteins also decrease would directly validate the proposed mechanism.

finding_title: EEF2 targeting induces a large Vgf, Nptx2, and Cx3cl1 trophic state in superficial cortical neurons
main_reason:
The work ranks high on novelty because EEF2 is already known to regulate protein translation, so translation-related effects are expected. However, a large Vgf, Nptx2, and Cx3cl1 induction specifically in superficial cortical neurons was not previously expected.

The support, however, is incomplete. The "Support" section mentions that Eef2 RNA was not significantly reduced (FDR significant), hence, successful perturbation was not demonstrated. They also did not measure EEF2 protein, elongation rates, or ribosome activity. Therefore, it remains uncertain whether the observed gene expression changes are a direct consequence of EEF2 disruption or are secondary effects. consequentl I ahve marked it as low priority.
excited_community: Dr. Lei Shi, JNU‐HKUST Joint Laboratory for Neuroscience and Innovative Drug Research, College of Pharmacy, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China. Their work (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535807/) indicates their interest in EEF2, neuronal protein translation, and excitatory synaptic function.
followup_programs: The most promising experiment would be to validate EEF2 protein depletion by Western blot. The protein translation can be measured using a puromycin incorporation assay to confirm that the observed gene expression changes are a direct consequence of EEF2 disruption.

finding_title: NR2F1 perturbation couples Sorl1 induction to Sema7a repression in thalamic Prkcd/Grin2c neurons
main_reason:
The finding is partly novel because NR2F1 is already known to regulate brain development (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8715095/). The new part is the proposed association with Sorl1 and Sema7a in adult thalamic neurons, which was not previously expected.
The biggest limitation is that Nr2f1 itself was not significantly reduced (FDR = 1.0). Therefore, successful perturbation was not demonstrated. In addition, only two genes showed significant changes, so, the proposed perturbation effect is limited and could be indirect. Hence, I marked it as weakly supported and low priority.
excited_community: Dr. Michèle Studer. Université Côte d’Azur, CNRS, Inserm, iBV, Nice, France. Their research (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8715095/) indicates their interest in NR2F1 and its role in brain development, neuronal specification, and cortical development.
followup_programs:
The most promising experiment would be to confirm NR2F1 knockdown at both RNA and protein levels using qPCR and Western blot, then use qPCR to test whether Sorl1 is induced and Sema7a is repressed after NR2F1 loss.
Grant: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). It supports research on neuronal development. Since NR2F1 is implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, this is a good fit.

finding_title: Dctn1 loss selectively activates a neuronal sterol-biosynthesis program
main_reason:
The findings suggest that the loss of DCTN1 triggers a cholesterol biosynthesis program, rather than producing only transport-related defects. This finding is novel. DCTN1 is already known for its role in axonal transport and its involvement in Perry syndrome, ALS, and frontotemporal disorders (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5546300/). However, a coordinated cholesterol biosynthesis response following DCTN1 loss was not previously expected. 

The data support is incomplete. The findings claim that Dctn1 loss resulted in a concerted induction of Insig1, Msmo1, Hmgcs1, Fdps, Ldlr, Hmgcr, Nsdhl, Fdft1, Sc5d, and Sqle. The "Support" section, however, doesn't include statistically significant data confirming induction of Nsdhl, Fdft1, Sc5d, and Sqle genes. 

I marked it as High Priority because DCTN1 is a known disease gene for Perry syndrome, ALS, and frontotemporal/parkinsonian disorders (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5546300/). The additional link to cholesterol biosynthesis makes this finding significantly more important.
excited_community: Dr. Ruben J Cauchi. Centre for Molecular Medicine and Biobanking, Biomedical Sciences Building, University of Malta, Msida, Malta. their work (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2023.1164251/full) indicates their interest in DCTN1, axonal transport, and ALS disease mechanisms.
followup_programs: A simple experiment would be to knock down Dctn1 in neurons and measure cellular cholesterol levels using a cholesterol assay. If cholesterol increases after Dctn1 loss, it would support the RNA data showing activation of cholesterol-biosynthesis genes

finding_title: Srsf1 loss elicits a pan-neuronal splice-factor autoregulatory response
main_reason:
The main finding is that the loss of SRSF1 causes a broad, pan-neuronal disruption of the splicing network rather than a cell-type-specific effect. I have marked Novelty as "known biology.." because Srsf1 is already known to be a master splicing factor that regulates its own expression and influences many other splicing regulators.
