Broad transcriptional effects after SRSF1 loss have been reported before. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7897272/).

I have marked it as a high priority. SRSF1 is a central splicing-regulator, and RNA-splicing defects are implicated in many neurodevelopmental disorders (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12182228/). Furthermore, the data support is strong: Srsf1 perturbation affected nearly 9,000 genes, with consistent responses across all 23 neuronal cell types.
excited_community: Dr. Auinash Kalsotra. Department of Biochemistry, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA. Their research (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-35932-3) indicates their interest in SRSF1, RNA splicing, and the cellular consequences of SRSF1 deficiency.
followup_programs:
I cannot assess the promising experiments to follow.

Grant: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). It supports research on RNA splicing. Since SRSF1 is a central splicing regulator and splicing defects are linked to diseases such as ALS and frontotemporal dementia, this is a good fit.

finding_title: BRAF and MAP2K1 perturbations repress, whereas NF1 perturbation induces, a neuronal VGF-PTPN5-ETV5 MAPK module
main_reason: The polarity is what MAPK biology predicts and the finding concedes as much and the module members are canonical pathway readouts rather than surprises, ETV5 is a direct ERK-family target and STEP/PTPN5 sits in a documented reciprocal relationship with ERK1/2, since STEP knockout raises ERK1/2 phosphorylation (PMID 21501258). Support is nonetheless strong because 3 activating-arm perturbations (Braf, Map2k1, Shoc2) all lower Vgf while the pathway's negative regulator Nf1 raises it with the NF1 arm recurring in two additional classes; a bidirectional sign flip is much harder to produce by artifact than a one-directional signature, which offsets the fact that neither Braf nor Map2k1 shows FDR-significant self-depletion.
excited_community: RASopathy and neurofibromatosis research, specifically the neurocognitive arm would be interested on this. This is where the finding has traction, because MEK inhibition (selumetinib) is already approved for NF1 plexiform neurofibroma and the cognitive consequences of chronic pathway modulation are an open clinical question. Also NF1 learning-and-memory groups working Ras-pathway effects on synaptic function, the Children's Tumor Foundation, and STEP/PTPN5 biology labs given that PTPN5 moves coherently in both directions here. I cannot provide particular names without extensive searching.
followup_programs: The stated gap is that no MAPK activity was measured, so the decisive experiment is phospho-ERK1/2 immunostaining or Western in the same sorted thalamic population after each perturbation, which converts a transcript polarity into a pathway measurement. Because Vgf is neurotrophin- and activity-responsive, the leading alternative is that the polarity tracks neuronal activity rather than direct MAPK output; pairing the perturbation with activity clamping (TTX or chemogenetic silencing) would separate those. Confirm Braf and Map2k1 protein loss, since neither self-transcript is FDR-depleted, and test whether pharmacological MEK inhibition phenocopies Map2k1 targeting, a result that would also directly address the selumetinib cognitive question. This would be great for an NINDS or NCI R01 on cell-resolved neuronal MAPK output in RASopathies, with Children's Tumor Foundation support for the NF1-specific arm, using Vgf/Ptpn5/Etv5 as branch-selective pharmacodynamic biomarkers.

finding_title: KLF7 perturbation links Tuba1a repression to a thalamic cytoskeletal transcript pattern
main_reason: A single gene passes FDR at log2FC −0.281 while six of seven "aligned" genes fail, several badly (Map6 FDR 0.690, Dctn1 FDR 0.748), and Klf7 itself is unchanged at FDR 1.0 with the canonical Ntrk1/CDKN/Rac3 outputs absent, the finding's own conclusion that this could be one marker plus correlated noise is the correct reading. KLF paralog effects on neuronal morphogenesis and axon growth are established (PMID 19815778), so even a validated cytoskeletal direction would be unsurprising.
excited_community: KLF-family axon growth and regeneration labs such as Murray Blackmore (Department of Biomedical Sciences, Marquette University) and Jeffrey Goldberg (Byers Eye Institute, Stanford University School of Medicine), who established paralog non-equivalence. Realistically, none would pursue this as presented; it is a perturbation-validation item, not a finding.
followup_programs: The gap is that no perturbation was demonstrated, so confirm KLF7 protein loss by immunoblot before interpreting anything downstream. If real, KLF7 CUT&RUN would test whether Tuba1a is a direct target, and the sub-threshold cytoskeletal genes require properly powered replication rather than reinterpretation of nominal values. Tubulin protein levels and live microtubule-dynamics imaging would test whether a −0.28 log2FC transcript change has any structural consequence, my expectation is that it does not. No standalone funding is warranted; at most a validation sub-aim within an existing KLF-and-axon-growth award.

finding_title: SIN3A targeting induces cilium and cholesterol genes while repressing spliceosome transcripts in thalamic and midbrain neurons
main_reason: Sin3a RNA is significantly increased after its own perturbation (+1.354, FDR 2.36e-17) and rises in 4 further classes, so loss of function is not demonstrated in any context, and most of the module is composed of genes that respond to unrelated perturbations elsewhere, Odf2, Dzip1, and Hcn3 lead the KLF9 signature, while Srrm2 and Snhg11 move after Trrap, Ogt, U2af2, and Naa20, which argues for a shared nuclear-state signature rather than a SIN3A-specific program. SIN3A haploinsufficiency in Witteveen-Kolk syndrome and SIN3A's role as an HDAC scaffold are established prior work; the cilium-plus-cholesterol-plus-spliceosome combination is the unexpected element, but it is the part least separable from the state-shift alternative.
excited_community: Witteveen-Kolk syndrome clinical genetics and the SIN3A/HDAC corepressor field, plus neuronal chromatin groups working postnatal SIN3A function. The most likely genuine pull is the CYP46A1 arm, which interests brain cholesterol-turnover researchers because CYP46A1 is pharmacologically activatable by efavirenz and is in trials for Huntington's and Alzheimer's, an unexpected chromatin route to that enzyme would matter to them even if the rest of the module does not survive. Maybe Dr. Lance Johnson, Department of Neuroscience at University of Kentucky College of Medicine, would be interested in such data.
followup_programs: The finding cannot proceed until SIN3A protein loss is demonstrated, since the transcript moves the wrong way, immunoblot plus a degron-SIN3A comparison would settle whether these guides do anything. To address the promiscuity problem directly, re-derive the signature after regressing out the shared cross-perturbation module (Srrm2, Snhg11, Rsrp1, Odf2) and ask what remains SIN3A-specific. If the cholesterol arm survives, measure 24S-hydroxycholesterol by mass spectrometry, since Cyp46a1 transcript change without flux change is uninterpretable; if the cilium arm survives, image primary cilia directly. SIN3A CUT&RUN would test direct occupancy at Cyp46a1 and Hcn3. NICHD or NINDS R01 on postnatal SIN3A function in Witteveen-Kolk syndrome, with the CYP46A1 axis as a potential therapeutic entry point given existing pharmacology, would be obvious choices.

finding_title: Zfp423 loss disrupts Grid2ip/Cd47 and derepresses Ntsr1 in Prkcd/Grin2c thalamic neurons
main_reason: A postnatal thalamic role for ZFP423 has no precedent I could find, the cited prior work is cerebellar (PMID 16943432, PMID 28893945), but the evidence has an unaddressed alternative: Grin2c, a defining marker of the 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut class, falls while Ntsr1, a marker of a distinct thalamic/corticothalamic population, rises +5.14 (roughly 35-fold) from only 160 perturbed nuclei. Loss of a class-defining marker alongside massive induction of a foreign one is as consistent with cell-identity drift, doublets, or ambient contamination as with derepression, and the finding attributes the concern to marker sparsity rather than to assignment.
excited_community: ZFP423/ZNF423 developmental biology and Joubert-syndrome-related ciliopathy genetics, which currently frame this gene almost entirely through cerebellum. Thalamic circuit and cell-taxonomy groups would engage because the Ntsr1 result is, if real, a claim about identity boundaries in their classification. There is also an adipose-biology community around ZFP423 as a preadipocyte determination factor that would find a neuronal identity-maintenance role conceptually parallel to its known role in commitment.
followup_programs: The alternative explanation and the validation experiment are the same one: single-molecule FISH for Ntsr1 together with Grin2c and Prkcd on tissue sections, which distinguishes genuine derepression within Grin2c-positive neurons from contamination by Ntsr1-positive cells. I would run doublet detection and ambient-RNA correction on the same data as a computational check. Report Zfp423 self-depletion, which is currently absent. If derepression is confirmed, ZFP423 CUT&RUN would test direct occupancy at the Ntsr1 locus, and conditional postnatal Zfp423 deletion with electrophysiology would test whether Grid2ip and Grin2c loss alters thalamic synaptic properties. This would be great for NINDS R01 on postnatal maintenance of thalamic neuronal identity by a factor previously confined to cerebellar development, a strong story if and only if the FISH comes back clean.

finding_title: Prdm10 perturbation reveals a conserved Madd, Cadm3, Ptov1, Stmn2, Myt1, and Uchl1 repression signature
main_reason: PRDM10 is genuinely understudied, I did a search on it and PubMed returns fewer than 30 papers on it overall, and I found no neuronal Prdm10-to-Madd/Cadm3 precedent while the evidence structure is the strongest in this assignment, Madd significant in 10 of 10 classes, Cadm3 and Ptov1 in 9, with q values to 8.7e-42. Recurrence across ten independently sampled neuronal populations is a far better control against class-specific artifact than concordance among correlated perturbations, and it is the reason this survives despite no reported Prdm10 self-transcript row. The main overreach is calling the set a "mature axonal and cell-adhesion module" when MADD (a DENN-domain Rab3 GEF), CADM3 (adhesion), PTOV1 (transcription), MYT1 (TF), and UCHL1 (deubiquitinase) are functionally heterogeneous.
excited_community: PRDM-family chromatin biology, where PRDM10 is the least characterized member and an atlas-derived functional handle would be immediately useful. Also MADD/Rab3 presynaptic trafficking labs, since Madd is the most reproducible hit and links to release machinery, and cancer genomics groups working PRDM10 fusion-driven soft-tissue tumors, who would want to know what the wild-type factor normally maintains. Not a particular name stood out in my search to report without extensive search
followup_programs: Because the reproducibility is already strong but directness is not established, the priority is PRDM10 CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq across two or three of the ten responsive classes, asking whether Madd, Cadm3, and Ptov1 promoters are directly bound, cross-class recurrence plus shared occupancy would make this a genuine regulon rather than a correlated module. I would report Prdm10 self-depletion and confirm protein loss. Because the signature is compact, deeper sequencing or a degron for acute kinetics would test whether the narrow output reflects true target specificity or limited sensitivity. Functionally, MADD loss predicts a Rab3-dependent release defect, testable by mEPSC recording and pHluorin imaging. An NIGMS or NINDS R01 on PRDM10 as an uncharacterized maintenance factor for neuronal adhesion and trafficking genes is of high interest, the kind of gene-to-function gap that R01 review panels reward when the reproducibility is this clean.

finding_title: CTCF perturbation robustly represses clustered protocadherins in thalamic and midbrain neurons
main_reason: This is exact precedent, not a new relationship. Hirayama et al. showed that conditional CTCF deletion in postmitotic projection neurons markedly reduces clustered Pcdh isoform expression (PMID 22854024), which is the same gene family, the same direction, and already in postmitotic neurons, so even the "mature-neuronal" framing is not new. The evidence is nonetheless excellent and the interpretation is scoped exactly to it, coordinated repression across α, β, and γ clusters at log2FC −1.1 to −2.5 in two independent classes is essentially unfakeable and the finding correctly presents itself as a positive control rather than a discovery.
excited_community: Clustered protocadherin and neuronal identity groups would be interested. Takeshi Yagi (Graduate School of Frontier Biosciences, Osaka University), whose lab produced the original CTCF conditional knockout, and Tom Maniatis's lineage on stochastic Pcdh promoter choice. Also 3D-genome and CTCF/cohesin labs interested in benchmark datasets, and the atlas producers themselves, for whom this is the validation case.
followup_programs: The scientifically interesting question is not the Pcdh arm but whether single-cell isoform choice diversity collapses, which requires isoform-resolved single-cell sequencing rather than aggregate abundance, precisely the measurement Hirayama could not make and this platform could. The unexplained Zcwpw2-up and Dennd6b/Abhd14b-down branch should be tested against other chromatin perturbations in the same atlas to determine whether it is CTCF-dependent or a generic state shift. Use this finding as the platform benchmark rather than a grant target, then fund the isoform-choice question as an NINDS or NIMH R01 on stochastic protocadherin coding of neuronal identity.

finding_title: KMT2A perturbation reveals a mature thalamic Nr2f1-Pcdh7-Lhx9 maintenance state
main_reason: Kmt2a is part of the maintenance of mature neurons, but the established target in the literature, Meis2, is missing (PMID: 25834037). I do not see any direct connection of Kmt2a with Nr2f1, Pcdh7 and Lhx9, so this could be real and a plausible change in target due to cell type. Some of the interpretation is based on genes for which no evidence is given (Camk2d, Grik2 and Cx3cl). For the given genes in the dataset, there appears to be strong enough support to merit follow-up investigation. However, the gaps in the support make it hard to be confident that any follow up investigation would be valuable. I would suggest doing a follow up time permitting, but not interfering with any other major projects (Moderate priority).
excited_community: Groups focused on the COMPASS complex will likely want to follow up on this finding. Historically, I would have recommended the Bryk Lab at Texas A&M University, but I believe they have retired, so the Klose Lab at Oxford is probably the next best choice.
followup_programs: Since the Kmt2a target is so well defined, a CUT&RUN-seq experiment could readily test for enrichment and deenrichment of H3K4 methylation in the identified gene loci. I would also recommend repeating the KO of other COMPASS components to identify if they phenocopy Kmt2a KO, to validate that the results. I don't think this model and predicted function would qualify for any cancer research (but might be able to be spun into a cancer proposal). I think this might be best pursued in developmental biology contexts, this would open the funding sources such as the NSF & NIH, but also target the number of new research foundations for aging & regeneration.

finding_title: Elp1 perturbation activates an amino-acid starvation and integrated-stress-like program in thalamic glutamatergic neurons
main_reason: The induced gene set seems to be the core elements of the integrated stress response (ISR) (PMID: 27629041, PMID: 39505107). I believe the claim, slightly reworded/simplified to be clearer, is: KO of Elp1 induces potential ribosome stalling, mirroring amino acid starvation, due to absence of Elp1 modifications. If this is a proper interpretation, the literature cited in the finding supports Elp1 involvement in neurons (PMID:24917501, PMID:35481599). To that end, the connections appear to be logical and well supported by the data. This tells me that the signal is likely valid. As such, I would recommend this be followed up on quickly, as it is probably going to produce positive data quickly (High priority).
excited_community: This work seems very in line with the Slaugenhaupt Lab at Harvard Medical School for studying familial dysautonomia. The literature of the finding also suggested another strong lab, the Lefcort lab at Montana State University (cited in the finding PMID: 35481599), due to the closeness of the target cell and existing research.
followup_programs: To prove the ICR is activated, the use of an ATF4-reporter would be a rapid test to prove ICR involvement. Though the ICR is a broad response, it would be best to confirm Elp1 involvement directly, with Ribo-seq in a time course in order to identify if tRNA modification is causing stalling events. If the Ribo-seq experiment fails, the follow up experiment should be a complete proteomic analysis to identify the proteins effected by the wobble codon modification and if the pool of those proteins begins to shift in behavior or function. Due to the strong support and the strong connection to the existing literature, I am convinced that there is a real finding here. The existing connection to disease, familial dysautonomia, might be enough to ask the associated foundations for an endowment, but I would recommend a grant from the NSF for a more general study and see where the research starts pointing.

finding_title: Apc loss activates canonical Wnt feedback in Prkcd/Grin2c thalamic neurons
main_reason: This appears to be the textbook example of Wnt derepression (PMID: 23169527, PMID: 28916710), where Wnt derepression activates components of the APC/β-catenin destruction complex to create a negative feedback loop to initiate degradation. As such, the statement in the finding of being a "clear positive control" is valid. The only notable flaw in the dataset is that Notum appears to be lacking an FDR value. The genes identified outside of the  APC/β-catenin destruction complex (Atrnl, Serpine2, Gls and Bace2), through a quick title search, appear to be Wnt correlated (PMID: 39329089, PMID: 39687341, PMID: 31196962, PMID: 39217971). I don't think there is any follow up needed, as it appears to be a positive control, but could be used to validate other members of a KO library as the technique can work on known data. I would agree that this is a valid experiment to run, but not something that needs to be followed up on and can be repeated as a positive control in conjunction with other experiments (No priority).
excited_community: This is what appears to be a positive control experiment. Thus, it is marketable as a control to other labs (industrial and academic), but is not something that needs following up on. If I were to stretch the limits of what can be done with this cell line, because of Wnt's role in cancer, this could be used as a background or test lineage in thalamic glioma groups; then Labs like Mathios Lab at Washington University might have a use in that context.
followup_programs: As the finding appears to  suggest this is  a test/control for Wnt derepression, follow up should not really be necessary. Though if individuals were interested, most of the studies I saw that correlated non-APC/β-catenin destruction complex genes to Wnt (PMID: 39329089, PMID: 39687341, PMID: 31196962, PMID: 39217971), I did not see any evidence of direct interactions. Therefore, a ChIP-seq analysis might be a good follow up. I doubt there is anything here to seek funding for, as it is part of the established literature, just in a new cell line. It might be relevant for Turcot syndrome (I think that is due to inherited mutations of APC, though) or thalamic glioma groups, and thus foundations targeting this research (e.g. Thalamic Glioma Registry) might fund or purchase this cell line.

finding_title: NAA20 perturbation couples recurrent CYP46A1 repression to induction of sterol-synthesis transcripts
main_reason: Doing a quick review of the literature, there is no explicit relationship between Naa20 and Cyp46a1. The provided evidence doesn't seem to even really support the claim, as the evidence as there isn't a convergence on a consistent set of genes. This is also contrary to literature that would support the null hypothesis (PMID: 29073233). The claim is shaky at best, but would be novel if true. I would not encourage following up on this finding, but due to the suspect nature and my inability to fully disprove the claim, I would suggest following up only if there are no more pressing interests in the lab  (low priority).
excited_community: As I can't find strong support for the claims or an underlying logic, it is hard to recommend any lab. A larger generalist group, such as the BRAINS Research Lab at UT Health Houston, or a similar group, might be ideal, as they are multidisciplinary. However, due to the Cyp46a1 literature, this could likely get pitched to an Alzheimer's or Huntington's research team as well.
followup_programs: I would test for N-terminal acetylation of Cyp46a1 in a proteomic screen, comparing before and after a Naa20 knockdown to evaluate if Cyp46a1 is a direct target of Naa20 activity. I also think a metabolic screen should be done to validate that the sterol maintenance is sufficiently disrupted. I don't believe this finding is ready to be presented to any funding agency at this time, but the best grant would probably be from the NSF or an endowment from an Alzheimer's or Huntington's foundation.

finding_title: MATR3 perturbation induces an RBP state that active FUS and TDP-43 perturbations do not reproduce
main_reason: This appears to be logically connected and partly redundant to existing literature (PMID: 40707625). The convergence of MATR3 and FUS to REST-UNC13A, the reported prior expectation is valid, but by not giving a source, this made it seem like a logical extrapolation instead of a known relationship. The other reported set of genes (Atp9b, Ddhd1, E2f4, Kcnq2, Sugp2, Uggt2, Rsrp1, and Zkscan3) appear to be novel in relationship, but are logical connections. So aside from the finding lacking a relevant citation, both the hypothesis, justification and data appear to be sound. I would recommend this finding get top priority for follow up experimentation, as it will likely add valuable data to the field rapidly (Exceptional priority).
excited_community: I would target a group with ALS-FTD-focused research. Under that subset, a large group such as the MassGeneral Institute for Neurodegenerative Disease (MIND) would likely have the resources and diversity of team members to follow up rapidly on this finding.
followup_programs: The first experiment that needs to be followed up on is long-read RNA sequencing with novel splicing analysis. The pathway converging on splicing means that splicing needs a complete evaluation. Next, I would suggest CLIP-seq with a MATR3 target to identify all direct targets of MATR3. Then a follow up evaluation for secondary, tertiary and background effects might be causing the other identified DE genes. The evidence is strong enough to start applying for NIH and ALS foundations for funding immediately, as the data is independently strong and the hypothesis is supported by the literature.

finding_title: Sec63 perturbation induces an ER-chaperone response distinct from selected secretory-pathway perturbations
main_reason: Chaperone induction is a logical unfolded protein associated response, but the identified DE is surprisingly weak considering the logic of the connection (PMID: 292639, PMID: 33006969). This is likely due to insufficient or unreliable knockdown/out of Sec63 (lacking a significant FDR). But due to the availability of literature, we can agree that the response is probable, but not certain. Another issue is the "distinct" claim, as not enough evidence is given in this finding to qualify the response to Sec63 (if it was properly perturbed) from the other selected transcripts (Ssr4, Stt3b and Ergic1). I would hinge the priority as being moderate if the team is able to confirm Sec63 perturbation through an orthogonal measurement, but this is due to the strength of the literature, not the reported results (Moderate priority).
excited_community: Researchers who specialize in ER-proteostasis, like the Oakes Lab at the University of Colorado, are going to be the best served by this, as ER work is rather specialized compared to the common cytosolic analysis. There is also a case, due to the cell line, to suggest this to teams studying neurodegeneration as well.
followup_programs: With the existing cell line, utilizing an established assay to measure unfolded protein levels would give more credibility to the data than can be demonstrated by an insignificant perturbation of Sec63. If there is indeed accumulation of unfolded proteins, a proteomic screen to test for Hspa5, CanX, Hyou1 and Chac1 induction would be an important addition show that the response is not just transcriptional. I would also suggest having an orthogonal KO for Sec63 in order to establish the level of the perturbation and potentially add more modulation to the severity of the perturbation. This work is likely able to seek funding as a neurodegeneration model and can likely get funding from Alzheimer's foundations, NIH (I speculate the findings are to weak to get an NIH grant though) and the NSF.

finding_title: U2af2 perturbation depresses spliceosomal and calcium-handling genes in thalamic and midbrain neurons
main_reason: The claim of a "distinct spliceosome-to-synaptic-homeostasis" is not specific enough to be novel, and the list is dominated by splicing-related genes, which is not surprising, although the direct relationships described here do appear to be novel. The claim is not well supported, primarily because U2af2 itself is not reported to be downregulated. Additionally, the claim that these represent "spliceosome-to-synaptic-homeostasis" is tenuous at best as only a few of these genes are tangentially related to synaptic transmission. This claim in the core idea differs from the title which references depression of calcium-handling genes, which is also not supported as there is only Atp2a2 on this list. Furthermore, multiple genes listed in the claim (Srsf11, Iffo1, Copb1) are not listed in the support.
excited_community: This finding would be broadly interesting to the field of RNA splicing. Additionally, U2AF2 has been implicated in childhood brain and development issues and this would be interesting to the the neurodevelopment field, and has been implicated in blood cancers and so this would be interesting to cancer biologists. Kathi Zarnack at the University of Wurzburg studies alternate splicing using high-throughput and bioinformatic methods and would likely be interested in these findings.
followup_programs: The experiment would need to be repeated with guides that reliably downregulate U2af2. Then differentially spliced genes should be determined to help elucidate which genes are misregulated due to spliceosomal stress and which are listed as misregulated due to differential splicing. This would be likely to be funded by government grants, such as from NINDS and NIH, as well as blood cancer related funding such as Blood Cancer United.

finding_title: Tpr loss induces a nuclear-transport transcriptional program centered on Ranbp6 and Xpo1
main_reason: The claim that "partial nuclear-pore disruption is sensed as an RNA-export or nucleocytoplasmic-transport stress" is unspecific and obvious and therefore not novel. The list of genes provided do appear to be novel results after Tpr perturbation, although some of them (like Xpo1) are known to have a functional relationship and thus are not surprising. It's unclear why CHD9, which was mentioned in the support, is not mentioned in the overall claims, particularly given the presence of transcription factors in this list. The claim overall is weakly supported since downregulation of Tpr itself is not reported in the support. Additionally, based on the support provided, there seems to be little overlap between different cell types, further casting doubt on the claim.
excited_community: This finding would be of broad interest to scientists studying nuclear export, and some genome integrity groups as TBR loss has been shown to lead to R-loop accumulation. Additionally, this would be interesting to scientists studying neurological disorders as TPR mutations have been implicated in neurological disorders causing intellectual disability and microcephaly. This finding would be likely to be pursued by Marco Foiani at IFOM Istituto Fondazione di Oncologia Molecolare in Italy who has studied TPR and how it relates to RNA-mediated replication stress.
followup_programs: The experiment should be repeated with different guides to ensure adequate downregulation of Tpr at the RNA and protein level. If the results are confirmed, the misregulated genes should be compared to those under perturbation of CHD9, ZFP770, and ZFP281 to determine if these constitute a transcriptional program that results in the misregulation of the other genes under TPR perturbation. This would be likely to be funded by neurological-related mechanisms, like NINDS at NIH, as well as mechanisms to study genome integrity, like NCI or NIEHS at NIH.

finding_title: ADNP perturbation defines a CHD4-adjacent neuronal signature across thalamic, midbrain, caudal GABAergic, and Pvalb populations
main_reason: ADNP is known to regulate Vstm2l (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-020-00904-4) but the rest of the relationships listed here appear to be novel. However, since ADNP is a transcription factor known to be active in the brain a significant gene signature is not surprising. The evidence here is weak since the gene expression changes after CHD4 perturbation is not reported and would need to show similar patterns as ADNP perturbation to demonstrate that these claims are due to the ChAHP complex. Additionally, the downregulation of ADNP is not reported here.
excited_community: ADNP is implicated in multiple neurological disorders, primarily Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, but also autism and thus this finding would be interesting to neurodevelopmental scientists. For example, Roy Ben-Shalom at UC Davis has studied ADNP in the context of neurodevelopmental disorders and would likely be interested in these findings.
followup_programs: The experiment should be repeated with a variety of guides to insure downregulation of ADNP at the transcript and protein level. Then this could be compared to a similar experiment with perturbation of CHD4 to delineate the contribution of the ChAHP complex. This could motivate research funded at the MIND Institute at UC Davis which is already working of ADNP-driven diseases like autism.

finding_title: PPP2R1A perturbation reverses sterol-transcription polarity across neuronal classes
main_reason: The claim that PPP2R1A perturbation results in different "sterol-transcription polarity across neuronal classes" would be a novel claim. While PPP2R1A is known to effect SREBP1 and therefore transcription of cholesterol-related genes, opposite effects in different neuron types would be novel. This claim is not well supported as downregulation of PPP2R1A itself is not shown, nor is the effect on SREBP1, the key mediator of this pathway, making these claims impossible to properly interpret. Additionally, one of the downregulated genes, HMGCR has an unimpressive fold change and FDR, and SREBP2 is another regulator and this downregulation could be due to a number of feedback mechanisms.
excited_community: This would be interesting to scientists that study cholesterol biosynthesis especially in the brain, as well as the field of neurodevelopment as PPP2R1A can cause Houge-Janssens syndrome 2. Gesine Saher at the Max Planck Institute studies perturbations in cholesterol metabolism and how this affects the nervous system using mouse models and would likely be interested in this finding.
followup_programs: The experiment should be repeated with different guides to ensure downregulation of PPP2R1A at both the RNA and protein level. If the results hold true, SREBP1 and SREBP2 levels and activity (via reporter system) should be determined see if there are different effects on these regulators in different cell types. This would likely be funded by both basic science mechanisms such as NINDS at NIH, as well as foundations such as Alzheimer's Disease Drug Discovery Foundation given the link between cholesterol metabolism in the brain and Alzheimer's.

finding_title: YLPM1 perturbation lowers Srsf6-Srsf5 and Inha in midbrain-linked neurons
main_reason: The role of YLPM1 in the brain, as well as the association with Srsf6, Srsf5, Inha, and the upregulated genes listed here does not seem to have been studied and is quite novel. YLPM1 is already known to associate with ribonucleoprotein complexes and splicing factors however. The findings are consistent and well supported as there are multiple splicing factors downregulated in 155 MB Glut. Additionally, Ylmp1 is reported to be downregulated in several cell types, which adds a critical control support.
excited_community: YLPM1 seems to have an association with RNA-binding proteins as well as a role in TERT regulation, making this finding interesting to RNA biologist as well as scientists who study genome integrity. Mark Mattson at Johns Hopkins studies aging and telomeres in neurons and would likely be interested in this finding.
followup_programs: A key follow-up experiment would be to confirm that YLPM1 perturbation lowers protein levels in these cells types, as well as confirming that it is expressed before perturbation. It would also be interesting to determine the cellular location in these cell types (i.e. colocalization with nuclear speckles and/or telomeres) before and after perturbation. This would likely be funded by basic research programs through NIH or NSF.

finding_title: AP2M1 and AP2S1 perturbations converge on TFRC induction and sterol repression while AP2S1 adds cortical activity-gene loss
main_reason: This claim conglomerates three separate claims without a cohesive hypothesis: induction of an iron-uptake signal, induction of lipid-regulation, and an "activity-output branch". TRFC is a transmembrane protein internalized by AP-2, so upregulation of Tfrc with AP-2 perturbation is not surprising but apparently unreported. AP-2 is known to be important for LDL uptake, but this specific observation of reduced sterol-regulatory transcripts upon AP2M1 and AP2S1 perturbation appears to be novel. The claim of an "activity-output branch" involving Arc/Egr3/Bdnf/Vgf is vague, and some of these are known to directly interact with AP-2, but these specific relationships have apparently not been described. The Tfrc claim is well supported as downregulation of Ap2m1 and Ap2s1 was reported and the induction of Tfrc was seen in both perturbations and multiple cell types; the evidence for Srebf2 is slightly weaker as it is only reported for one cell type. The evidence for Arc/Egr3/Bdnf/Vgf is much weaker since it was only reported for Ap2s1 perturbation in one cell type.
excited_community: This finding would be of interest to the field of drug discovery for brain-related conditions, since the transferrin receptor is a target of drugs that need to cross the blood brain barrier. This finding would likely be pursued by Zheying Zhu at the University of Nottingham who studies drug delivery methods like transferrin for diseases like Alzheimer's.
followup_programs: A key follow up experiment would be to determine if the induction of Tfrc leads to an increase in the transferrin receptor at the protein level, and if so, if iron import into the cell is properly maintained by this increase. This would likely be funded by government grants through NINDS at NIH, or industry funding given the drug delivery implications.

finding_title: PPP2R1A perturbation defines a cortical Amy1-high, Rsrp1/Leng8-low reporter state with TSC/STXBP1 neighborhood structure
main_reason: While FDR percentages are significant for the genes identified in this perturbation study, the fold changes of the affected genes besides Amy1 are modest, all under +/- 1 log2FC. Given those results, I am cautious about the confidence for this finding, combined with a previously known link between PP2A-related intellectual disability and mutations in other proteins related to glycogen breakdown and metabolic control in neurons, which makes these results potentially incremental and not unprecedented (PMID: 26576547).
excited_community: The researchers most interested in the signature changes for these intratelencephalic glutamatergic neurons would be other notable researchers studying the effects of PP2A-related intellectual disability. Wendy L Chung from the Columbia University Medical Center has published a related paper on GSK3β-mediated cell growth in the context of PPP2R5D de novo mutations (PMID: 26576547). An industry partner that would be interested in these findings is GeneDx, which specializes in genetic testing for rare diseases, and has published a paper on a variant in PPP2R5C as it is related to (PMID: 39696819).
followup_programs:
The most promising followup experiment in my mind would be to strengthen the obvious biological connection between these identified gene families. The connection between the only significantly upregulated gene Amy1 and the TSC/STXBP1-positive and LIMK1/DNAJB6-negative states appear to encompass many potential (and confusing) biological contexts. Therefore, I would like to show some epistatic relationship to determine what are the direct targets of PPP2R1A perturbation. 

Mutations in PPP2R1A cause Houge-Janssens syndrome 2, an autosomal dominant disease causing developmental delay and a range of muscular/skeletal defects including microcephaly. Therefore I think some of the appropriate funding bodies would be through the NIH’s initiative to fund the Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network, considering Houge-Janssens syndrome 2 is classified as a rare disease. The Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network has 21 research consortia and $26 million dollars in grant funding since 2025.

finding_title: PGK1 and GAPDH perturbations converge on OGT and nuclear-speckle transcript loss
main_reason: Both PGK1, TPI1, and GAPDH are proteins that carry out their roles in glycolysis, and this analysis showed a decrease in Pgk1 with Pgk1 perturbation but not a GAPDH decrease upon GAPDH perturbation, which raises the first of two concerns with this experiment. The second concern raised in the evaluation is that cellular stress is the main driver for these results, especially due to the extremely minimal log2FC values for all of the spliceosome/speckle markers listed, and therefore my interpretation for these results is lackluster.
excited_community: One of the more comprehensive communities for research into nuclear architecture was funded by the NIH Common Fund between 2015-2025 called the 4D Nucleome (4DN) program. While this consortium recently ended, it represents researchers from in the U.S. and around the world who are still active in research studying the 3D organization of the nucleus as it changes over time. Notable members of 4DN who would find research into nuclear speckles relevant are Teresa Szczepińsk from CEZAMAT Warsaw University of Technology, Carolyn Larabell from UC Berkeley, and Thoru Pederson from UMass.
followup_programs:
The most relevant followup experiment I would conduct, beyond verification of the perturbation result, would be to visualize nuclear speckles upon PGK1 or GAPDH perturbation. Assaying RNA fold changes from spliceosome complex members alone is not sufficient to make any claims on the presence or absence of dynamic speckles; therefore, an immunostain against Y12 (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles) or an TEM image to look at protein density (at interchromatin granule clusters) in the nucleus would be an appropriate starting point to see if speckles change compared to a control. 

The National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) as part of the NIH has previously funded several UM1 grants (Research Project with Complex Structure Cooperative Agreements) that focus on larger-scale programs or consortium. This style of grant is appropriate for projects that require the expertise of multiple research components and were often granted as part of the 4DN program. While that research focus has ended, perhaps resuming this style of research to tackle complex interactions between a subset of glycolytic enzymes and RNA processing mechanisms.

finding_title: Rnpc3 loss creates a core spliceosome response centered on Mapk8, Ap2a1, Wdfy1, Pcyt2, and Pten
main_reason: The numerous genes identified in this screen, many of which are involved in key maintenance pathways like JNK and PTEN, are strongly up- and downregulated upon Rnpc3 perturbation, which provides strong evidence for followup mechanistic study. The hypothesis is that perturbations in RNPC3 cause intron retention in specific pathways from dysregulation of the U11/U12 minor spliceosome complex, which has substantial evidence from the identified perturbation experiments and by previous knowledge of the function of the minor spliceosome (PMID: 38484052) and is worth further investigation.
excited_community: Alternative splicing plays a large role in generating RNA isoforms which are essential in the nervous system. Many researchers devote time and energy in studying isoform usage in disease and cancer, but the most relevant researchers for these findings would be notable researchers who study the effects of RNA isoforms on development and disease pathobiology in the CNS, examples being: Jeremy Kay and Simon Gregory from Duke University and Hagen Tilgner from Weill Cornell Medicine.
followup_programs:
The followup experiment I would suggest would be in line with the proposed idea to look at long-read sequencing to assess if there was a difference in intron retention upon RNPC3 perturbation. I would specifically propose to look at a targeted long read single-cell experiment using Twist probes against the top, stringently changed genes (236 stringent genes in 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut and/or the 221 genes in 155 MB Glut, 77 in 052 Pvalb Gaba, 73 in 066 CNU-HYa HY GABA, and 55 in 191 MB P MY GABA) along with Pacbio Kinnex sequencing. By using a targeted approach for known exons of your genes of interest, you are able to sequence deeper than a whole-transcriptome approach and you recover longer transcripts than a poly-dT pulldown method. In this experiment, you would look for intron retention in the perturbed datasets compared to controls. 

The research programs that would fund this endeavor would include PacBio itself - the company has proposals for yearly SMRT grants, where they award HIFI sequencing runs to labs after submission of a short proposal. Additionally, since I think the findings for these results are worthy of followup, I would target NIH institutions for 00/R01 awards for independent labs from the NINDS, NIMH, and NICHD institutions.

finding_title: BMAL1-CLOCK and REV-ERB perturbations recover an asymmetric neuronal circadian feedback loop
main_reason: The concept that a pooled group of similar cells will be in sync with the phase of its circadian clock gene expression is not groundbreaking, and I agree with the interpretation that the priority for a followup experiment is low to moderate. However, I agree that the results are strong and that they align with what is known about the CLOCK/BMAL1, PER/CR,Y and REV-ERB feedback loops and therefore have scientific backing to be legitimate.
excited_community: In 2017, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to three members of the circadian clock field Jeffrey C. Hall (Brandeis University), Michael Rosbash (Brandeis University), and Michael W. Young (Rockefeller University), all of whom have interest in future discoveries in this field. There are many more researchers than those who won academia’s most notable prize - including Joseph Takahashi from University of Texas Southwestern who discovered the mammalian Clock gene.
followup_programs:
One of the most promising followup experiments I would suggest is the most obvious, but also the most needed experiment, which is to gain time resolution to this claim. Collecting multiple time points over a 24-hour cycle will permit a visualization of the amplitude of the asymmetric Dbp and Nr1d2 output upon Bmal/Clock perturbations and compare with the Nr1d1 or Nr1d2 perturbations and the change with Dbp. 

Howard Hughes Medical Institute has funded multiple notable circadian clock research programs over the years, and is a funding source I would target for funding in this field. To this end, at the postdoctoral stage, HHMI has recently revamped their Hanna H. Gray Fellows Program to be more inclusive to postdoctoral researchers at multiple stages (up to 7 years of postdoctoral time) and would be a good target for this work. For graduate students in their PhD work, HHMI has the Gilliam Fellows Program which provides three years of funding.

finding_title: STXBP1 perturbation produces distinct cortical, midbrain, and Pvalb transcriptional outputs
main_reason: The identified genes have lackluster fold changes under 1.00 in the layer 5 intratelencephalic-projecting glutamatergic neurons, MB Glutamatergic neurons (except for Mt1 and Fos), and the Pvalb+ GABAergic interneurons. While I am more confident in these results when perturbations lowered their own transcripts (as in Stxbp1 and Slc6a1), I am hesitant to draw significant conclusions with these data due to the low fold changes, but am interested in the holistic picture of neuronal stress and would consider follow up studies.
excited_community: Interested researchers for this study would be Mingshan Xue from Baylor College, who works on gene therapy approaches for STXBP1 disease, and Matthijs Verhage from VU University Amsterdam, who has authored 43 scientific papers on STXBP1/Munc18-1 since 2020. Multiple, additional researchers are identified on the STXBP1 Foundation website, and would be of consideration for this project.
followup_programs:
The most promising follow up study I would propose for this work is to untangle the presynaptic vesicle release phenotype that is known in the literature with the new, stress-induced response. My first experiment would be to include the stress response independent of the vesicle phenotype with stepwise perturbations of the identified downstream targets of STXBP1 perturbations, and assess if there is a comparable seizure phenotype as seen in the canonical STXBP1 pathways.  

Mutations in STXBP1 account for one of the five most common genes linked to epileptic encephalopathies and other neurological disorders. There is a STXBP1 Foundation which has a grants program focused on funding basic biological mechanisms of STXBP1 disease. Relevant to this study, there are small Seed Grants that would be most relevant to this work, funding up to $25k of direct costs for a year.

finding_title: Kansl1 loss perturbs midbrain lysosomal and Golgi trafficking transcripts
main_reason: This identified signature of KANSL1 haploinsufficiency in the midbrain is representative of a solid finding that will likely advance the field forward in understanding how autophagy malfunction affects neurons specifically. While the novelty score is lower for a hypothesis such as this, the support this evaluation has in the 39 affected stringent genes is strong.
excited_community: Koolen-de Vries syndrome is caused by a 7q21.31 microdeletion and is a relatively newly discovered, rare genetic mutation. There is a foundation that supports research for this syndrome by the same name. Researchers who are supporting their mission include Marina Colombi from the University of Brescia in Italy, and Bert B A de Vries from the Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands.
followup_programs:
The first experiment I would do would be to attempt to rescue the KANSL1 haploinsufficiency phenotype in specific midbrain cells with a KANSL1 rescue experiment delivered via AAV or comparable viral infection into a knockout mouse. Rather than a global rescue, I would be interested in the acute response to cellular trafficking within the affected population, which could be read out by a number of methods (immunohistochemistry, electron microscopy). 

The NIH NIMH is interested in rare genetic variants that lead to changes in neurodevelopment, and would be a good funding agency to target for Koolen-de Vries syndrome. Figuring out how KANSL1 haploinsufficiency acutely alters turnover of membrane proteins in autophagy would be beneficial to begin to understand exactly what phenotypes of the disease are most critical to tackle for something like gene therapy, which could be targeted to specific midbrain cells to restore critical function. At other U.S. funding agencies, there are opportunities through the NIH NINDS and NICHD with R01/F32/F31 funding.

finding_title: Rab7 loss elicits a lysosomal hydrolase and sterol-response state
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 1 indicates that Rab7 loss leads to more than a 2-fold increase in Scpep1 and Dusp1, between 1.5- and 2-fold increase in Insig1, and less than a 1.5-fold increase in Atp6v1b2 in thalamic neurons (151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut) as well as a 1.5- to 2-fold increase of Grn and Lamp2 and less than a 1.5 fold increase in Mcoln1 in midbrain neurons (155 MB Glut) with Dpp7 increased more than 1.5-fold but less than 2-fold and Atp6v0b increased less than 1.5-fold in both thalamic and midbrain neuron classes. Rab7 is a well-estasblished RAS-related GTPase “that controls vesicular transport to late endosomes and lysosomes in the endocytic pathway” with causative mutations in CMT2B (Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2B) disease, an axonal neuropathy (PMID: 19754445), and is a late endosomal marker that is increased along with Lamp2 in Machado-Joseph diseased brains (PMID: 29218765) and associated with “midbrain dopaminergic neurons in GBA1-linked Parkinson's disease” (PMID: 33753743). These data and other published works support the interpretation that “Rab7 loss elicits a lysosomal hydrolase and sterol-response state” and there is a demonstrated mechanistic link between Rab7 loss and increased neuronal sterol levels (PMID: 36623732).
excited_community: Research groups investigating the role of sterol metabolism in CMT2B, Machado-Joseph, and Parkinson’s diseases are most likely to pursue this finding. Specific investigators include Drs. Anna Maria Giudetti, Cecilia Bucci, and Flora Guerra at the University of Salento.
followup_programs: The strongest follow up experiment is to conditionally increase Rab7 in 151 TH Prkcd Grin2c Glut and 155 MB Glut thalamus and midbrain neurons and interrogate gene expression, with reciprocal expression changes to those described in the finding supporting a relationship, followed by an assessment of neurological phenotypes. Potential funding agencies include the American Parkinson Disease Association (APDA), CaixaResearch Institute at “la Caixa” Foundation, Charcot-Marie-Tooth Association (CMTA), CMT Research Foundation (CMTRF), and the NIH (NINDS).

finding_title: Acute TBR1 perturbation recurrently raises CPNE6 while splitting mature cortical projection-neuron outputs
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 2 indicates that Tbr1 perturbation decreases Dkk3 and Epb41 more than 2-fold in layer 5-6 intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, with Dkk3 reduced between 1.5- and 2-fold in layer 4-5 IT neurons, and increases Cpne6 at least 1.5-fold in all three neuron classes with more than a 2-fold increase in layer 6b olfactory bulb neurons along with Cacna1a. Tbr1 is a transcription factor with well-established roles in cortical neuron development, including layer 6 axonal projections, and mutations are associated with autism spectrum disorders (PMIDs: 26578866, 32005960, 35781633). Cpne6 has established roles in long-term potentiation and dendritic spine morphology (PMIDs: 27194588, 28158493). While both are brain-specific proteins and pertain to neuron plasticity, the relationship described in the finding appears novel and the stated interpretation about separate Tbr1 roles in neonatal fate-specification and projection-neuron identity is plausible, but there is an unexplained disconnect between Tbr1, Cpne6, Dkk3, Epb41, Cacna1g, and C1qtnf4 as the following pairwise PubMed searches return zero results: Tbr1 Cpne6; Tbr1 Dkk3; Tbr1 Epb41; Tbr1 Cacna1g; Tbr1 C1qtnf4; Cpne6 Dkk3; Cpne6 Epb41; Cpne6 Cacna1g; Cpne6 C1qtnf4; Cacna1g C1qtnf4; Dkk3 Epb41.
excited_community: Research groups investigating the molecular mechanisms of autism spectrum disorders or memory are most likely to pursue this finding. Specific investigators include Dr. Matthew State and Dr. John Rubenstein at UCSF.
followup_programs: The strongest follow-up experiment is to connect Tbr1 and Cpne6 in cortical projection neurons by generating a double knockout animal model (maybe conditional KO), examining physiological changes in brain structure and architecture, and using standard neuroscience assays to assess cognitive phenotypes. Potential sponsors include the Autism Centers of Excellence (ACE) under the NIH COMBINE Program, DOD CDMRP, and Autism research foundations (e.g., Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative).

finding_title: HSPA8 perturbation induces a compact HSP70-HSP90 compensatory transcript arm
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 3 indicates that Hspa8 loss leads to more than 1.5-fold increases of Hsp90aa1 in a class of hypothalamic neurons and Dnaja1 in a class of layer 2-3 intratelencephalic neurons with both increased less than 1.5-fold in a class of thalamic neurons that have at least a 1.5-fold increase of Cct6a and ~1.3-fold increase of Hspa4l. Hspa8 is a well-established member of the Hsp70 chaperone family, a family antagonized by the co-chaperone Dnaj1a (PMID: 22343013). A compensatory increase in Dnaja1 and Hsp90aa1 following Hspa8 loss is in agreement with published research showing that increased Dnaja1 and Hsp90aa1 activity promotes tau clearance (PMIDs: 22343013, 38247340). The interpretation accurately reflects the supporting data, stating that “loss of constitutive HSPA8 releases a compensatory folding response,” meaning an increase in Dnaja1 and Hsp90aa1, without overstating proteasome correlations or proteostasis recovery.
excited_community: Research groups investigating chaperone compensation mechanisms in tauopathies and Alzheimer’s disease are most likely to pursue this supportive finding. Specific investigators include Dr. Laura Blair USF Health Byrd Alzheimer’s Center and Research Institute and Dr. Marc Diamond at UT Southwestern Medical Center.
followup_programs: The strongest follow-up experiments are to determine if Hspa8 loss promotes tau clearance, modulates protein folding, or leads to other phenotypic outcomes. Potential research sponsors include the Alzheimer’s Association, BrightFocus Foundation, NIH (Center for Alzheimer’s and Related Dementias (CARD), NIA, NINDS), and Rainwater Charitable Foundation (RCF).

finding_title: Ogt loss represses RNA-processing and cholesterol-turnover transcripts while relieving Xpo1
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 4 indicates that an approximate 3- to 5-fold Ogt loss in two midbrain neuron classes leads to more than a 2-fold increase in Xpo1 and ~2-fold decrease in Rsrp1 with more than a 2-fold decrease of Cyp46a1 in the GABAnergic class and ~1.9- to 2.4-fold decrease of Odf1, Kifc2, Srrm2, and Leng8. Ogt is an O-GlcNAc transferase and O-GlcNAcylation has well-established roles in neurodegeneration, neurodevelopment, and synaptic transmission modulation (PMIDs: 33300544, 37229433, 37349834, 38167470) as do RNA-processing, cholesterol metabolism, and nuclear export. However, a direct connection between the identified genes appears to be novel as there are no PubMed results for the following pairwise searches: Ogt Xpo1; Ogt Rsrp1; Xpo1 Rsrp1; Ogt Leng8; Ogt Srrm2; Ogt Odf2; Ogt Kifc2; Ogt Cyp46a1; Xpo1 Cyp46a1; Xpo1 Leng8; Xpo1 Srrm2; Xpo1 Odf2; Xpo1 Kifc2. The interpretation that Ogt is “a bridge between metabolic sensing and RNA homeostasis” and “is required in postnatal neurons to maintain RNA-processing factors and cholesterol-turnover transcripts” is plausible, but incomplete and somewhat overstated given only the correlative expression described in the finding without metabolic, O-GlcNAcylation, or RNA-processing experimental measurements.
excited_community: Research groups investigating Ogt-related molecular mechanisms of brain aging, dementia, and neurodegeneration are most likely to pursue this finding. Specific investigators include Dr. Suzanne Walker at Harvard Medical School and Dr. Thomas Schwarz at Boston Children’s Hospital.
followup_programs: The strongest follow-up experiments are to experimentally measure cholesterol metabolism, O-GlcNAcylation, and RNA-processing after conditional Ogt loss in the named midbrain neuron classes. Potential research sponsors include the Alzheimer’s Association, American Brain Foundation, Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) Institute of Aging, and NIH (NIA, NINDS).

finding_title: Distinct endomembrane perturbations converge on a proteostasis-associated neighborhood with node-specific outputs
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 5 indicates that Atp6v0a1 perturbation reduces Atp6v0a1 ~1.5-fold in three neuron classes (thalamic, Glutamatergic midbrain, parvalbumin), PI4KA perturbation reduces Slc12a5 more than 1.5-fold in a GABAnergic midbrain neuron class, and CAML perturbation increases Stmn4 more than 2-fold in the GABAnergic midbrain neuron class as well as between 1.5- and 2-fold in the parvalbumin neuron class. The shared “many-to-one neighborhood” of ATP6V0C, CAML, PI4KA, DHDDS, VPS53, and VPS54 “with node-specific leading outputs: ATP6V0C lowers Atp6v0a1, CAML raises Stmn4, and PI4KA lowers Slc12a5” appears to be novel as there is only one PubMed result for “Atp6v0a1 ATP6V0C” and none for the following pairwise searches: ATP6V0C CAML; ATP6V0C Stmn4; Atp6v0a1 CAML; Atp6v0a1 Stmn4; CAML Stmn4; PI4KA CAML; PI4KA Stmn4; Slc12a5 CAML; Slc12a5 Stmn4. The interpretation may be plausible but is incomplete as the connection “rests on correlation and low-count marker finding” without causation or even expression correlation after the same perturbation.
excited_community: Research groups investigating the molecular mechanism and physiology of neuronal networks and their microenvironment are most likely to pursue this finding. Specific investigators include Dr. Shelley Halpain at UCSD.
followup_programs: The strongest follow-up experiments are to conditionally perturb both ATP6V0C and CAML GABAnergic parvalbumin neurons or CAML and PI4KA in GABAnergic midbrain neuron as described in the finding and then assess both gene expression and neurological phenotypes. Potential funding mechanisms include NIH NIA- or NINDS-sponsored grants requesting projects investigating the physiology and local microenvironment of neuron classes with close proximity.

finding_title: Zbtb11 perturbation recurrently lowers Rbm28, Stx16, Acsf3, and Ndufaf1 across subcortical neurons
main_reason: The information provided in Part I finding 6 indicates that Zbtb11 perturbation decreases Acsf3, Pigq, Rbm28 and Stx16 more than 2-fold in a glutamatergic thalamic neuron class with Stx16 similarly reduced in a glutamatergic midbrain neuron class and Acsf3 similarly reduced in a GABAnergic midbrain neuron class where Ndufaf1 is reduced more than 4-fold. Zbtb11 is a zinc finger transcription factor associated with intellectual disability (PMID: 29893856) and the “reduced binding of the mutated ZBTB11 to ACSF3 leads to decreased ACSF3 transcript level” (PMID: 35104841), reflecting the finding’s supporting data. A relationship between Acsf3, Ndufaf1, Rbm28, Stx16, and Zbtb11 appears novel as the following pairwise searches produce 0 PubMed results: Zbtb11 Rbm28; Zbtb11 Ndufaf1; Rbm28 Stx16; Rbm28 Acsf3; Rbm28 Ndufaf1; Stx16 Acsf3; Stx16 Ndufaf1; Acsf3 Ndufaf1. The “interpretation that functional ZBTB11 disruption couples nuclear control of mitochondrial capacity to nucleolar, glycan, and endomembrane maintenance” is plausible, but incomplete, and is an overstatement based on correlative expression but the stated significance, “If…real…would give ZBTB11-associated intellectual disability a tractable multi-compartment neuronal mechanism…linking mitochondrial output, ribosome biogenesis, membrane trafficking, and glycan biology” is scientifically sound given the individual molecular identities.
excited_community: Research groups investigating the molecular mechanisms of ZBTB11-associated intellectual disabilities are most likely to pursue this finding. Specific investigators include Dr. Vlad Seitan at King’s College London.
followup_programs: The strongest follow-up experiment is to confirm these correlations by performing the opposite Zbtb11 perturbations and interrogating gene expression as described in the finding. Those genes that show significant fold increases (i.e., reciprocal expression) are valid targets to pursue in functional studies that examine neurobiological phenotypes. Potential funding agencies include the Foundation for Children with Intellectual and Development Disabilities, The John Merck Fund, and NIH (Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network (RDCRN), NICHD, NINDS).

finding_title: Arid1a, Smarcb1, Smarcc2, and Smarce1 perturbations converge on Ptpn3-Reep2-Prkcd repression with Clstn2-Nexn induction
main_reason: Variants in ARID1A, SMARCB1, SMARCE1 and SMARCC2 cause Coffin-Siris syndrome with intellectual disability (doi: 10.1002/ajmg.a.62889). All four are cBAF subunits and their variants cluster in shared structural regions of the complex (doi: 10.1038/s41588-023-01451-6). Neither study examined neurons. In the finding, all four perturbations lowered Ptpn3 in thalamic neurons, while Arid1b did not. Partial precedent.  Arid1a, Smarcb1, Smarcc2, and Smarce1 levels are not reported in the finding, hence these perturbations are not verified and the effects seen in the findings cannot be attributed to Arid1a, Smarcb1, Smarcc2, and Smarce1. Because the perturbations could not be verified, the priority to take this finding forward cannot be determined.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying cBAF subunit variants in neurodevelopment disorders, such as the Kadoch lab at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. 
2. Labs studying de novo SMARCC2 variants, such as the Campeau lab at the University of Montreal.  
3. Labs studying Coffin-Siris syndrome genetics, such as the Clinical genetics hub at Seattle Children's research institute.
followup_programs:
Promising experiments
1. Measure Arid1a, Arid1b, Smarcb1, Smarcc2, and Smarce1 RNA and protein levels. Also sequence the guide site, to verify whether the perturbations worked. 
2. Confirm the protein expression of each gene altered in the finding including Ptpn3.
3. Map BAF binding on Ptpn3 in thalamic neurons to determine if it is a direct target. 
4. Use an orthogonal method such as siRNA knockdown in thalamic neurons to verify the findings of perturbation.


Research programs
1. NIH BRAIN initiative, since the response is restricted to a defined neuronal class. R21. 
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, since ARID1A, SMARCB1, SMARCE1 and SMARCC2 variants cause Coffin-Siris syndrome. R01.
3. National Institute of General Medical Sciences, to understand the role of the BAF complex in neurons. Specific aim in a larger grant.

finding_title: PPP3CA and PPP3R1 perturbations expose a noncanonical calcineurin transcript output opposite AP-2 adaptor states
main_reason: De novo  PPP3CA mutations were identified in six individuals with severe developmental delay and refractory seizures (DOI: 10.1016/j.ajhg.2017.08.013). The study proposed PPP3CA mutations cause epilepsy by reducing dynamin-1 dephosphorylation and endocytosis. In fission yeast, catalytic domain mutations blocked Prz1 dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation (https://doi.org/10.1093/hmg/ddy052). Neither study examined thalamic neurons. The gene changes observed in the finding have not been reported. Partial precedent. Ppp3ca and Ppp3r1 decreased after perturbations, hence perturbations are verified. PPP3CA variants cause a refractory epileptic encephalopathy, hence the priority is moderate to high.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying PPP3CA variants in developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, such as the Mefford lab at the University of Washington. 
2. Labs studying functional consequences of PPP3CA mutations in a yeast model, such the Mizuguchi lab at Yokohama City University Graduate School of Medicine. 
3. Labs studying endocytosis and synaptic vesicle recycling such as Haucke lab at the Leibniz-Forschungsinstitut für Molekulare Pharmakologie (FMP).
followup_programs:
Promising experiments 
1. Verify the protein levels of all the transcripts that have changed, to confirm the changes are translated to protein levels. 
2. Re-express wildtype Ppp3ca, a catalytic domain mutant or auto-inhibitory domains mutant in the perturbed neurons, to identify the domain required for the changes observed.  
3. Measure calcineurin phosphatase activity in the perturbed thalamic neurons. 
4. Perform double perturbation of Ppp3ca or Ppp3r1 with Ap2s1 or Ap2m1, to test whether the anticorrelation is epistasis. 

Grant-funded research programs
1. NIH BRAIN Initiative programs, since the work is done in specific neuronal cell types. R01. 
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, since calcineurin is linked to synaptic plasticity and psychiatric phenotypes. R01. 
3. CURE Epilepsy, since Ppp3Ca variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Specific aim in a larger epilepsy grant.

finding_title: Ranbp2 perturbation produces Srrm2-down/Rbm15-up cortical and Grm1-Epha4-Itpr1-up cerebellar responses
main_reason: Conditional Ranbp2 deletion in mouse spinal motoneurons caused hindlimb paralysis and death by day 10.5. The same deletion in Thy1 neurons of the brain produced no behavioral or physiological phenotype (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.027730). Ranbp2 loss therefore acts differently between neurons, which supports the finding. In the same mice Cxcl14 mRNA increased about tenfold while Cxcl14 protein decreased by half or more. This indicates that transcript direction did not match protein direction. However, the study was not conducted in cortical projection or cerebellar GABA neurons. The gene changes observed in the finding have not been reported in this cell type. Partial precedent. Ranbp2 decreased in cortical neurons, hence the perturbation is verified. No Ranbp2 is reported for the cerebellar neurons, hence the cerebellar response cannot be attributed to Ranbp2 and the priority for those neurons cannot be assessed.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying conditional Ranbp2 deletion in neurons, such as the Ferreira lab at Duke University. 
2. Labs studying endogenous Ranbp2 localization in neurons, such the Rasband lab at Baylor college of Medicine. 
3. Labs studying RanBP2 SUMO E3 ligase activity in cells, such as the Palazzo lab at the University of Toronto.
followup_programs:
Promising experiments
1. Measure Ranbp2 RNA and protein levels in both cortical projection and cerebellar GABA neurons. Also sequence the guide site, to verify whether the perturbation worked in the cerebellar neurons. 
2. Confirm the protein expression of each gene altered in the finding, since Cxcl14 transcript and protein moved in opposite directions after Ranbp2 deletion  
3. Re-express Ranbp2 constructs carrying loss of function in individual domains in perturbed neurons to identify which domain is required for the cortical and cerebellar responses (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.027730).


Research programs
1. NIH BRAIN Initiative, since the response differs between two defined neuronal classes. R21. 
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, since RANBP2 mutations cause acute necrotizing encephalopathy and Ranbp2 deletion in motoneurons produces ALS-like syndrome. R01.
3. Target ALS, since conditional Ranbp2 deletion in motoneurons is a LoF model of the disease. Specific aim in a larger grant.

finding_title: KLF9 perturbation defines a Wsb1/Rasgrp2/Pld3 thalamic module distinct from KLF7 and KLF13 outputs
main_reason: Klf9 is a thyroid hormone inducible TF required for late postnatal neuronal maturation. KLF paralogs can exert different effects on CNS genes. Klf9 bound the Klf13 promoter in mouse hippocampal neuronal cells and repressed Klf13 reporter activity (DOI: 10.1186/s12864-017-3640-7). Klf9 knockout in zebrafish larvae upregulated more genes than it downregulated (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-39453-3). Neither study was conducted in thalamic neurons. The gene changes observed in the finding have not been reported. Klf9 did not change, hence perturbation is not verified and the gene changes cannot be attributed to Klf9. Because the perturbation is not verified, priority cannot be assessed. Partial precedent.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying Klf family members: Denver lab at U of Michigan.  
2. The Goldberg lab at Stanford University, who showed Klf transcription factors in CNS axon growth. 
3. Allen Institute of Brain Science, since the finding is defined by specific thalamic cell class. 
4. Labs studying Klf9 loss in whole animal models, such as the Coffman lab at the MDI biological laboratory. 
5. Labs studying Klf9 and Klf13 paralogs in CNS gene network such as the Wegner lab at Friedrich Alexander Universitat.
followup_programs:
Promising experiments

1. Measure Klf9, Klf7 and Klf13 RNA and protein levels. Also sequence the guide site, to verify whether the perturbations worked. 
2. Confirm the protein expression of each gene altered in the finding.
2. Confirm whether the transcript changes are reflected at the protein level for Wsb1, Rasgrp2 and Pld3.
3. Double perturbations with Klf9 and Klf13, since the paralogs may compensate for each other. 
5. Determine whether the induced genes are direct Klf9 targets by CUT&RUN or ChIP. 

Research programs
1. NIH BRAIN Initiative programs, since the work is done in specific neuronal cell types. R21.
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, since Klf9 is required for late neuronal maturation. R21.
3. National Institute of General Medical Sciences, to understand how Klf9 paralogs regulate the same transcriptional targets in neurons. Specific aim in a larger grant.

finding_title: Wdr26 loss produces a cerebellar GABA channel-and-splicing signature
main_reason: WDR26 haploinsufficiency causes Skraban-Deardorff syndrome. It has been shown that WDR26 mutations impair CTLH/GID E3 ligase assembly and substrate interactions (DOI: 10.1002/1873-3468.14866). Wdr26 heterozygous mice display learning and memory deficits, social dysfunction, elevated seizure susceptibility and motor impairment (DOI: 10.1172/JCI195537). Neither study was conducted in adult cerebellar GABA neurons. The gene changes observed in the finding have not been reported. Partial precedent. Wdr26 levels are not reported in the finding, hence perturbation cannot be verified and the transcript changes cannot be attributed to Wdr26. Moderate priority because of Skraban-Deardorff syndrome, which is a rare disorder.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying WDR26 mutations and CTLH3 E3 complex assembly, such as the Murray and Alpi labs at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry. 
2. Labs studying Wdr26 heterozygous mice and Skraban-Deardorff phenotypes such the Xu lab at Nanjing Medical University. 
3. Labs studying Wdr26 in embryonic brain development, such as Yang lab at the Soochow University.
followup_programs:
Promising experiments
1. Measure Wdr26 RNA and protein levels. Also sequence the guide site, to verify whether the perturbation worked. 
2. Confirm the protein expression of each gene altered in the finding.
3. Perform patch-clamp electrophysiology on perturbed neurons. Cacna1g encodes a calcium channel and Kcnt1 encodes a potassium channel. The two transcripts moved in opposite directions in the finding. Measure resting membrane potential, input resistance, rheobase and action potential frequency to determine whether action potential generation in perturbed neurons differs from control. 


Research programs
1. NIH BRAIN initiative, since the response is restricted to a defined neuronal class. R21. 
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, because Wdr26 variants produce seizures and intellectual disability and no treatment exists. R01 or R21.
3. Skraban-Deardorff syndrome Foundation, to identify the role of Wdr26 in Skraban-Deardorff syndrome in cerebellar neurons. Specific aim in a larger grant.

finding_title: Thap11 perturbation reveals a conserved Rabac1-Sdccag8-Gdap1 mitochondrial/ciliary module
main_reason: It has been shown that Thap11 knockdown in adult mouse striatum and cerebellum does not reduce neuronal markers or Purkinje cell number (https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI178349) and that Thap11 binds Ndufa3 promoter and downregulates Ndufa3 in the developing retina (doi: 10.1016/j.celrep.2016.01.039). Neither study measured transcript in mature neurons. No study connects Thap11 to the genes in the finding. Partial precedent. Thap11 has no reported row, hence perturbation is not verified and changes observed in the finding cannot be attributed to Thap11. THAP11 CAG expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 51, so the priority to take this work would be moderate to high.
excited_community:
1. Labs studying THAP11 polyQ models and cerebellar degeneration, such as the Yang lab at Jinan University. 
2. Labs studying Thap11 targets and mitochondrial genes, such as the Poche lab at Baylor College of Medicine.
3. Labs studying Thap11 dosage in Purkinje cells, such as the Zwaka lab at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. 
4. Labs studying GDAP1 and mitochondrial membrane contact sites, such as the Palau lab at Institut de Recerca Sant Joan de Deu.
followup_programs:
Promising experiments
1. Measure Thap11 RNA and protein levels. Also sequence the guide site, to verify whether the perturbation worked. 
2. Confirm the protein expression of each gene altered in the finding.
3. CUT&RUN for THAP11 at the Rabac1, Sdccag8 and Gdap1 promoters in neurons 
4. Measure ATP and complex I, III, and IV subunits since Ndufa3 fell and it reduced ATP by 50% in retina. 


Research programs
1. NIH BRAIN initiative, since the same gene set changes across defined neuronal classes. R21. 
2. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, since THAP11 CAG expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 51. R01.
3. National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, since biallelic THAP11 mutation causes an inborn error of cobalamin metabolism with developmental abnormalities. R21.

finding_title: Rb1 and E2f4 perturbations release distinct replication and chromosome-repair arms in thalamic neurons
main_reason: There is sparse literature available on this topic in the field comparing replication vs repair in post-mitotic neurons. This concept would be of particular interest in the area of neurodegeneration/neurodegenrative disase, but the support for this particular finding is lacking. The evidence is at the transcriptomic level only, which cannot stand on its own in the absence of a functional, phenotypic. or protein-level readout. Angus et al (PMID: 15169903) provide partial precedent by demonstrating that RB1 inhibits DNA replication in fibroblasts, but this is an entirely different cell context that lacks comparison to the E2f4/DREAM arm.
excited_community: This finding is most relevant to the fields of neurodegeneration and neural repair (post-injury). Reversal of loss of postmitotic neurons due to disease or injury would have meaningful therapeutic applications for the treatment of TBI, ischemic disease, or neurodegeneration like Alzheimer's. This finding would be of particular interest to students and colleagues of the late Mark Smith, formerly at Case Western Reserve University, who study cell-cycle re-entry in AD pathophysiology, especially in thalamic atrophy.
followup_programs: First, confirmation of the transcript-level findings is needed from further perturbation experiments in primary thalamic neurons, which will need to delineate between replication and DNA damage repair with EdU incorporation and DNA-damage assays (gamma-H2Ax). From there, the most promising set of experiments to support this finding would be functional validation using ASOs or siRNA in vivo in an AD mouse model such as 5xFAD or APP/PS1 to study post-mortem impacts on synaptic density and gross neuronal atrophy. If the finding were to pursue Alzheimer's as a specific disease context, this finding and future studies would likely find success in foundation RFPs from disease-centric groups like the Cure Alzheimer's Fund or the BrightFocus Foundation. These foundation grants could be a bridge to a larger R01 or similar grants, but the finding needs to be confirmed in more mechanistic/fundamental studies to show promise for further development.

finding_title: ZMYM2 perturbation induces a Notum/Echdc2/F11r/Atp2a3 thalamic signature
main_reason: The finding itself describes the significance as "an incremental, low-priority extension of ZMYM2 chromatin biology." The finding reads more as a hypothesis for planning a set of next-step experiments, rather than as a cohesive research direction. There must be an experiment or set of experiments that functionally link changes in ZMYM2 expression or perturbation to changes in Notum signaling or Atp2a3-associated calcium handling. Graham-Paquin et al 2023 (PMID: 37395395) provides partial precedent where they generated a Zmym2 null mouse model that fails to undergo DNA methylation or germline silencing and shows upregulation of LINE elements, including a LINE-1 protein. This suggests a very important mechanistic role for this gene in murine embryonic development and global chromatin regulation, but the lack of functional or mechanistic evidence for this finding makes this topic interesting but underdeveloped.
excited_community: More basic science researchers who study chromatin regulation in neurobiology would be the most interested scientific community in this finding. As an RNA biologist with an interest in non-coding RNA, the prior precedent linking Zmym2 to LINE elements is of particular interest. However, there isn't much published research on Zmym2 expression in neuronal function or development specifically, and the fact that Zmym2 primarily interacts with SUMOylation makes it ubiquitous in terms of its role in widespread chromatin-associated silencing. This potentially limits its attraction for and application to translational research, limiting the interested field to a more mechanistic focus.
